utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. May I ask, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Than you. I take it the appearances are the same as yesterday. This is a fact. Then the question goes to Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez. Can you follow our proceedings in a language you understand? THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you for your kindness. Yes, I can follow today's proceedings in my language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can understand everything that is being said, and I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us continue without further ado. Let's be flexible with the time. You know the time allocated to the parties. Maybe not all the time will be needed in all aspects by the parties, so therefore let's be flexible. It should already now be said that the break -- that the lunch break today will take only one hour in order to conclude as scheduled. But first may I ask the parties in this case, Cerkez Defence and Prosecution, what about the still-open question of agreed facts in relation to the family situation based on the motion filed the 4th of May by the Cerkez Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If I may speak both on behalf of myself and Mr. Kovacic, we spoke this morning and went through the document. There are a few -- a few matters which remain somewhat contentious, and we've agreed to speak at the break again and we'll inform you, if you don't mind, this morning, but we'll try our best to find a way to get without having the Court's intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think it would be the best that I give immediately the floor to the Prosecution and the maximum time remaining would be one hour, but I take it maybe you don't need all the time. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will begin by attempting to answer the questions of His Honour Judge Guney and the questions by the Presiding Judge, His Honour Judge Schomburg's questions. Then I will make a few comments related to the submissions from yesterday, and then Ms. Jarvis will speak on the last aspects of our response to Mr. Cerkez's appeal. First of all, regarding the scope of the criminal plan, Your Honour. The geographic scope, the Trial Chamber in the judgement has adopted, which reflects the indictment, two levels of joint criminal enterprise or common plan. The first is that charged by -- excuse me, charged against the appellant Kordic, which is as the Court says at paragraph 827, Central Bosnia and beyond, meaning that it's the larger scope. It then finds that Kordic was involved in the larger scope at paragraph 829. In a subset of that persecutory campaign was carried out in the Vitez municipality, and that subset was the one that was for which Mr. Cerkez was found guilty, and the Trial Chamber confined his responsibility to the villages identified in the Vitez municipality. I'll make submissions in the Prosecution appeal that its confinement of Mr. Cerkez's responsibilities to only those attacks that it felt that the Viteska Brigade was directly involved in was in error. The crimes for which -- which was the subject matter of the criminal agreement. First of all, the Court has found that the overall objective was to subjugate the Bosnian Muslim population and that it was carried out or through the use of violent measures. The agreed upon measures to achieve this purpose - this is at paragraph 127 - was the attacking of towns and villages with the associated destruction and plunder, killing, injuring, and detaining Bosnian Muslims. I'll come to the question of what's outside the common plan in a minute, but that was found to be inside the common plan. And these objectives or the crimes agreed to carried out were exactly the same for the larger JC. The evidence disclosed, of course, that these acts were carried out in towns and villages and were replicated over and over again in a consistent pattern and were identical in each village. The carrying out of the plan on the evidence may have differed slightly and with different degrees of intensity, but the common denominator was the agreed upon attack of the village, the killing of injuring of those that were there, the destruction, the plunder, and then the detaining of the Bosnian Muslims, all taking place for the ultimate objective. The next question related to Mr. Cerkez's knowledge of the plan itself. There are two aspects to this in the Prosecution's submission. The first is that his knowledge can be inferred as a general matter from the evidence at large, and that relates to the ongoing plan and all the activities that took place in the Vitez municipality. He knew that there was a plan to target the Muslims certainly in the areas of Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska because he ordered his troops to go there and commit those crimes. He knew that the plan was greater than just those in the area for which the Trial Chamber found him guilty. It was clear that it was a coordinated military campaign, was carried out in conjunction with the Viteska Brigade, and that the acts for which the campaign were implemented were carried out by all the units in the Vitez municipality. I will make submissions on the evidence of the knowledge including things such as the small area in which it took place, the coordination that was required of the military units, the fact that, for example, the attack on Bosnia was the result of the efforts by the Vitez Brigade for blocking the Busovaca Brigade for blocking, and the artillery support from Hrasno hill from the Busovaca Brigade. This wasn't a individual act, uncoordinated and unknown to the other units who were standing by and acting in cooperation. There's also the evidence, which I won't go into great detail regarding the knowledge, but certainly the reports back to Blaskic relate to the whole area. It's inconceivable that the commander for the Vitez municipality, responsible for the whole area, responding back on Ahmici, Kruscica, Sivrino Selo, Vitez, Stari Vitez does not know what the specific plan is and the orders for one of those areas in his responsibility which is he to report back to. How is he reporting back to General Blaskic and how is General Blaskic asking him for reports on Vitez if he has no knowledge of what is actually happening there? His troops arrive there at the end of the day and carry out arrest operations. That's set out in the war diary, I think it's 1757. The arrest operations are in Ahmici by his troops. He doesn't arrive there with no knowledge of what's going on and what the purpose he's doing there for the arrest operation. He's reporting on our forces and he's reporting on them being 70 per cent done in Ahmici and Donja Veceriska. The only inference is that the 70 per cent relates to the activities in Ahmici, and the 70 per cent is not military operations. Secondly, in addition to the evidence, the broader evidence of -- which supports Mr. Cerkez's clear knowledge of the overall plan in the Vitez municipality is the evidence as the result of the meeting on April 15th. In the Prosecution's submission, even without the specific information, it would have been clear that the Trial Chamber would have been able to infer from the overall circumstances that he had knowledge; that was the campaign, that's what his troops were doing, that's the information that he was required to pass on. In addition we do have the information that on the 15th there was the plan, and the formulation of the plan, in terms of the units, and we have the information that the units that were there were Kraljevic, which were the Vitezovi; Cerkez, who is the Vitez Brigade; Ljubicic, who is the military police; and AT testifies to Grubesic being there who's the Busovaca Brigade. Those are all the units that took place in the Vitez municipality or the main ones, and when you look at that meeting you have Ljubicic who is the military police. Would General Blaskic give one set of orders to all the members who were at the military meeting, and then pull Ljubicic aside later and give him a second set of orders? If you accept the testimony of Witness AT, he says that Blaskic's orders are... This is not a separate activity devised by Ljubicic at a later time; it wouldn't make any sense that he calls his units together - the four main units that are engaged in the attack in the Vitez municipality, all of them reporting through the Vitez Brigade at least in terms of locations - and not tell the commander of the zone of responsibility what the orders are for one of the units? We also have information from AT that right beside Pirici, I don't know the size but it's literally -- couldn't be less than a kilometre is the units from the Vitez Brigade. And what's their responsibility? Their responsibility is to block UNPROFOR. Why would the Vitez Brigade be given a specific task to block an international organisation if it wasn't because they knew specifically what the operation was for? It's inconceivable that a military commander that gives the order that Blaskic gave would not tell the rest of the troops coordinating in a military operation what the order was. There's also information that Grubesic was there, at least in terms of AT's evidence. You will recall that the beginning of the Ahmici attack started with the shelling from Hrasno hill. That's the Busovaca Brigade. That's Grubesic, and he was at the meeting. You will recall that AT testified that UNPROFOR was also blocked from Kaonik, from the other side. He was blocked on the one side by the Vitez Brigade, and it was to be blocked on the other side by the Busovaca Brigade. That's Grubesic. Why would there be a order to block UNPROFOR from both sides from two different units if not for the fact that there was an illegal activity and illegal order going on. It's no coincidence they met on that day and all the units were given a coordinated attack and the knowledge can clearly be inferred as to what those orders were. Regarding the scope of the plan including the other crimes, first of all, the inhumane treatment under Count 31 which relates to the conditions of detention, if by inhumane treatment this refers to the conditions of detention, then no, the Trial Chamber did not find that this was part of the joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Cerkez was found liable on a separate basis in that regard. If the inhumane treatment is considered to be the trench-digging under Count 31, both being under Count 31, once again the Court finds that this falls outside of the common criminal plan. Regarding the hostage-taking, it's the same and the liability under count 33 is specifically for Mr. Cerkez. Regarding the deprivation of liberty. The Court actually found that the detention itself, the act of unlawful detention was a part of the common criminal plan. Regarding the mode of liability, the mode of liability for all those acts which fell within the common criminal plan which I've indicated is the unlawful attacks and the resultant destruction and activities, illegal activities, including detention, the mode of liability must be JC 1. In the Prosecution's submission, the Court didn't find it as aiding and abetting, or at least their conclusions were whether that's your legal characterisation but they did not find it aiding and abetting because the evidence discloses that Cerkez had much more than mere knowledge; he actually shared the intent for the JC. It's the Prosecution's submission that the JC could have been applied to various acts for example, the inhumane conditions. They could have been seen as foreseeable as a result of the detention, but it doesn't appear that the Trial Chamber found that. Lastly, His Honour Judge Guney asked about the liability for ordering. In paragraph 831, the Court concludes its findings in relation to the persecutory campaign and holds Mr. Cerkez liable as the commander of the Viteska Brigade as he participated in the attacks. They note that it's the high point of the campaign of persecution, and then he played his part in the campaign - this was his contribution - by commanding troops involved in some of the incidents. As such, he was a co-perpetrator. The word "commanding troops" has to be read as ordering. There is no other way that he would be involved in commanding troops. I note that the Court then concludes he's a co-perpetrator. For the joint criminal enterprise, it must be the co-perpetration with the joint criminal enterprise and that his role was to command the troops which, Judge Guney, I would submit, has to be ordering. Those are the answers to the specific questions. If there's any further questions, I'll be happy to answer them or I'll move on to the final issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these precise answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just add two more comments regarding the submissions by my learned friend, and then I'll pass the counsel table over to Ms. Jarvis. There has been, and Mr. Kovacic has been kind enough to give me a report regarding Mr. Cerkez while he's been in custody, and I understand if it's correct that Mr. Cerkez -- counsel for Mr. Cerkez will seek to file it, and I note it's before you. The Prosecution's position - though I take no issue with the fact that he may wish to file it and you can obviously have it before you - I would note that in your contemplation of the information in it, it relates to his detention from 1997 until the present. The Appeals Chamber in the recent decision on May the 7th, 2004, has concluded that evidence of post-sentence behaviour is irrelevant as to whether the Trial Chamber exercised -- erred in the exercise of its discretion, and the Appeals Chamber concluded that considering that the appellant's post-sentence behaviour could be neither relevant to any issue before the Trial Chamber, nor capable of being considered by it and therefore cannot show that the Trial Chamber committed any error in the exercise of its discretion, it therefore dismissed the Defence motion to have the post-sentence behaviour admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There was a question by Judge Weinberg de Roca, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farrell, about the meeting on April 15, has this meeting been an issue in other -- in any other of the related cases or has it only come up in this present case?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There -- there has been information, but it was in relation to closed session in another case and therefore I'm not at liberty to set out that material. There has been material that has been -- there has been material that has been filed in this case under the Rule 115 motion which this Court has excluded and found that the additional evidence could not affect the verdict. That evidence was filed in this case, but it was filed confidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just add one point. You correctly quoted from a recent judgement. However, we are in a slight dilemma. It's settled jurisprudence by the Appeals Chamber that for the purposes of the assessment, what about rehabilitation? It's necessary to know: Are they -- are there still links? What is the recent behaviour in the Detention Unit and so on and so forth. It's not a question whether the Trial Chamber made a mistake or not, but when, as it is true in this case, all parties are seeking for a new sentence, then this is no doubt a decisive factor, the question of rehabilitation and so forth. No doubt we need the necessary supporting information on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may just make a submission in that regard. If the Court upholds the sentence and if it finds that the Trial Chamber did not err, the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case has held that the post-sentencing conduct is irrelevant. The issue before you is whether the Trial Chamber erred. He doesn't get a second chance to have a reduction of sentence because he's been of good character since then. That's not a view in my respectful submission the Trial Chamber's judgement. The fact that he has asked for you to consider whether his sentence was appropriate doesn't put you in the position of a trial de novo; it puts you in a position, as I'm sure you're fully aware, of deciding whether the Trial Chamber was in error. If on the other hand this Chamber has to resentence him, in other words they have decided that they're going to change the nature of liability or decide themselves to resentence him unlike in the Celebici case where it was sent back to the Trial Chamber to resentence, then this Court may seek that information, but it in my respectful submission, the conduct for which he should be sentenced and the role of the sentence is to place him where he -- in the appropriate range of sentence for his crimes. The relevance of post-sentence behaviour, in my submission, and this was the submission we made in the Celebici appeal, this goes to issues related to the execution of the sentence, the administration execution of a sentence, that if he has done well in prison he will get certain benefits in prison. If his conduct -- post conduct is positive, that will assist in determining whether he's released at two-thirds. That isn't a consideration on determining whether his sentence was appropriate for the crimes he committed. Those were the submissions we made in the Celebici case, and that's the basis in my understanding of the ultimate decision in both Celebici and in the Kvocka case. Thank you. Those are essentially the matters that I wanted to bring to your attention. Thank you. I'll now, with your permission, ask Ms. Jarvis to address the last aspect of the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Jarvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. To begin, in response to Your Honour Judge Schomburg's question regarding the findings of Mr. Cerkez's discriminatory intent in the judgement: The findings are set out in paragraphs 830 and 831. In a nutshell, the Trial Chamber inferred his intent from his participation in the persecution campaign. Is that permissible? Yes, it is. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal is clear. Where all of the evidence reveals that this is the only reasonable inference, then the requisite mens rea can be inferred in this way. Indeed, in the vast majority in criminal cases, in the absence of some sort of express declaration by the accused, inference is the only way that intent can be proved. Paragraphs 830 and 831 are not expansive. But then again, they are conclusory paragraphs preceded by 800-odd other paragraphs in the judgement detailing the voluminous evidence that enabled the Trial Chamber to arrive at that point. Certainly the Appeals Chamber has demonstrated on two recent occasions, the Vasiljevic case and the Krstic case, a concern about the evidentiary basis that will be sufficient to enable intent to be inferred from the accused's knowing participation in a crime. About the dividing line between aiding and abetting on the one hand and participation in a joint criminal enterprise on the other. Why is the case of Mr. Cerkez different to those two cases? Well, in Vasiljevic, the Appeals Chamber was not satisfied that the accused knew about the criminal purpose to murder the Muslim men on the bank of the Drina River until a short time prior to the acts taking place, and his conduct thereafter in the Appeals Chamber's view did not unequivocally demonstrate that he had adopted that shared intent. He was, if you like, in the dark about the purpose of the other participants in the enterprise until right at the last minute. Not so Mr. Cerkez. He had his eyes wide open. He knew full well that the objective of the attacks in which he was engaged and in which he engaged his forces was to target the Muslim population for the very reason of their membership in that group, and he went ahead and ordered them to carry out the crimes anyway. The Krstic case. Again, the Appeals Chamber expressing great caution about the circumstances under which knowing participation can lead to inference of intent. Although Krstic knew about the genocidal enterprise of the VRS Main Staff in Srebrenica, the Appeals Chamber considered that his acts of contribution were not unequivocal. As commander of the Drina Corps, he permitted the use of corps assets to assist in the killings, but he did not deploy the troops to actually commit any of the crimes. Not so Mr. Cerkez. It was his troops, under his command, in his zone of responsibility, on the ground in Donja Veceriska, Vitez, and Stari Vitez who were deliberately targeting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Muslim population with discriminatory acts. He didn't send them in with instructions to carefully target only military objectives. He sent them in with express orders to target Muslim civilians and Muslim houses. Croat civilians and Croat houses were excluded. There is nothing unequivocal about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I interrupt, because this is a core issue of the case. You just said he sent them in with express orders to target Muslim civilians and Muslim houses. Where would you find this in the judgement or in the evidence before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that must be the only inference available on the evidence. The Trial Chamber accepted that there was a coordinated plan of attack, and this goes to what my colleague, Mr. Farrell, has just outlined for you about the nature of the criminal plan. It comes from the fact that these corps crimes of the joint criminal enterprise were replicated over and over again in all of the relevant -- all of the villages, including in the Vitez municipality, including in those villages where Mr. Cerkez's Vitez Brigade was operating. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber noted, at paragraph 831, that the crimes in which the Vitez Brigade were involved represented the high point of the persecution campaign. It's the Prosecution's submission that it is no coincidence that the very worst atrocities happened in the zone of possibility of Mr. Cerkez, no coincidence that he was the brigade commander reporting back to Mr. Blaskic -- to Colonel Blaskic about the process or the progress of the campaign in Vitez, as demonstrated by the material set out in paragraphs 688 to 702 of the judgement. No coincidence that he was reporting on some of the villages where some of worst atrocities to took place, paragraph 689(d). Ahmici, 70 per cent done, Donja Veceriska, 70 per cent done. No, Mr. Cerkez knew full well that he was engaging himself and his brigade in a campaign and knew full well that he was reporting back to Colonel Blaskic about the progress of ethnic cleansing in the Vitez municipality. He had his eyes wide open, but he went ahead and did it anyway. I emphasise, Your Honours, that Mr. Cerkez was not acting in a vacuum. Every Bosnian Muslim and every Bosnian Croat living in the Lasva Valley throughout 1992 and 1993 knew the score. They knew about the increasing tensions between the two communities, knew the HVO takeovers of the municipalities throughout 1992 onwards were happening, knew about the increasing acts of violence and intimidation against the Bosnian Muslim population. Mr. Cerkez did not just step into Vitez municipality on 15 April 1993. He had first been the assistant commander of the Vitez staff, then assistant commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade from October 1992 until February 1993. That's at paragraph 594 of the judgement. And then from March 1993, he was the commander of the Vitez Brigade. He was there at the Ahmici barricade in October 1992, and more than one witness at trial attested to the fact that Mr. Cerkez made grave threats about burning the municipality down if the barricade was not removed. That's at paragraphs 532 to 533, and the Prosecution final trial brief at paragraph 93. And as relations deteriorated between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in January 1993, Mr. Cerkez threatened to shell Vitez if the ABiH did not accept the HVO demands. That's at paragraph 594. On the evening of 15 April, Mr. Cerkez attended the joint commission in incidents -- sorry, the joint commission in incidents and gave assurances leading to the belief that there would be no HVO attack. This is the evidence of Witness G, referred to in paragraph 609 of the judgement. The duplicity of this was not lost on the Trial Chamber at paragraph 610 where they noted that on that very afternoon, Cerkez had attended the meeting of the military commanders, Pasko Ljubicic, Anto Sliskovic, Darko Kraljevic, and Grubesic among them at which the attack in the municipality of Vitez for the next morning was planned. And consider, Your Honours, the role that Mr. Cerkez's brigade was given in respect of Ahmici, as my colleague Mr. Farrell has emphasised, to prevent UNPROFOR from getting into Ahmici. He knew very well that the orders were for ethnic cleansing. My apologies if I'm going too fast for the interpreters. The Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici later on the 16th of April, and participated in the arrests of the Muslim civilians there. Mr. Cerkez was reporting on the progress of the campaign in Ahmici. It was obvious to everyone who saw the aftermath of Ahmici that a massacre had happened there. Did Mr. Cerkez express any horror or outrage? Did he demand an explanation? Did he refuse to be associated any further with the HVO? He didn't do any of these things. Instead, in May 1993, we see Mr. Cerkez irritated again with the ABiH and issuing a threat to burn down Kruscica. That's at judgement paragraph 694. Consider also the evidence of Mr. Breljas set out in paragraph 807(i) of the judgement about the coordinated waves of plunder that the Vitez Brigade and the Vitezovi engaged in. Mr. Cerkez was the commander of the Vitez Brigade. What did he think was going on? Add to this to Mr. Cerkez's role in the detention and hostage-taking crimes. The fact that Mr. Cerkez, as commander of the Vitez Brigade, did nothing in the face of this mistreatment of the Muslim detainees is relevant in assessing his overall discriminatory intent at the time. What's more, there is of course evidence of Mr. Cerkez's direct personal contribution towards the mistreatment meted out to the detainees, and I refer to paragraph 784(b) of the judgement. And further in paragraph 801, the Trial Chamber accepted the evidence of Witness AT that Mr. Cerkez, as commander of the Vitez Brigade had sent Muslim prisoners for trench digging. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, no, Mr. Cerkez was not acting in a vacuum. He knew full well that a persecution campaign was being waged against the Bosnian Muslim population of Vitez, and he went ahead anyway and deployed his troops to carry out the very acts designated to violate the fundamental rights of the Muslims for no reason other than their membership in that group. Your Honour, if I could also just return briefly to the question you asked about where in the judgement would I find support for my assertion that Mr. Cerkez was directly deploying troops for the criminal acts on the ground. Again, in paragraph 830, the Trial Chamber's finding is that he engaged his units in the persecution. Your Honour, I submit there is no other reasonable interpretation of that than that he was, with full knowledge, deploying his troops for the very purpose of the core crimes in the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, if I might just raise one procedural matter. I referred to Witness AT's testimony regarding -- and it is a matter that would need to be redacted from the transcript at page 17, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please do the necessary, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Sorry, it would be the reference to the entire passage from that point onward. Thank you. I do apologise for that oversight on my part. Your Honours, just a final point. It doesn't matter whether Mr. Cerkez was motivated to act in this way because of personal -- because of personal ethnic hatred, because he derived personal satisfaction from the campaign, or because he wanted to keep his job. As the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber noted at paragraph 100: "Shared criminal intent does not require the co-perpetrator's personal satisfaction or enthusiasm or his personal initiative in contributing to the joint criminal enterprise." It cannot be that different standards of intent apply to members of organised military units. It cannot be that a individual who carries out acts with the object of violating the fundamental rights of a person for the sole reason of their membership in a political or religious group is excused because he wears a uniform and because he operates within a chain of command. Your Honours, would any of us be entertaining any doubt about Mr. Cerkez's shared intent if he was wearing civilian clothes at the time and had organised and instructed for a group of people to go in and commit these crimes? His command position is not a impediment to finding shared intent. In fact, it just makes his actions even more grave. As a commander, he was entrusted with a special responsibility as guardian of the standards of human decency during armed conflict, and he used that special position for precisely the opposite purpose. Your Honours, that concludes the remarks I wanted to make on the mens rea for persecution. I do have a couple of very brief comments on the international armed conflict issue. Actually, two points arising out of His Honour Judge Pocar's questions to my learned friend yesterday, and that is in regard to the overall control test. Your Honours, the reason why the Tadic Appeals Chamber found that the Nicaragua effective control test was not the correct one, well, the Appeals Chamber examined the state of the judicial practice and state practice and concluded that for the purposes of determining when to attribute the acts of a military or paramilitary group to a state, the relevant test in customary international law was indeed the overall control test. The Nicaragua effective control test, the Appeals Chamber concluded, was the correct test for other categories such as individuals or groups that were not organised, but not for the specific case of military and paramilitary groups. So the overall control test, the Appeals Chamber concluded, is customary international law and always was at the relevant time when these acts took place, and that's why the Appeals Chamber in Tadic accepted that the accused Tadic could be convicted on the basis of this test for acts that happened in 1992. Secondly, the relationship between this Tribunal and the International Court of Justice. This point has been previously dealt with by the Celebici Appeals Chamber at paragraph 24. The Appeals Chamber specifically rejected arguments that the Tribunal was bound to follow the International Court of Justice. There is no hierarchical relationship between the two bodies and no reason why this Tribunal was not entitled to come to a different conclusion about the relevant law. The nullum crimen sine lege argument, again already considered and disposed of by the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski, paragraphs 126 to 127. The Appeals Chamber stated that the nullum crimen argument in that case, which is identical in all material respects to the ones that Your Honours have heard in this appeal, reflected a misunderstanding of the principle. There is nothing in the principle that prevents the interpretation of the law through decisions of a court. The very same assessment applies to the arguments raised by Mr. Cerkez. Mr. Cerkez has made very few submissions on the voluminous evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber to conclude that the armed conflict was international. In particular, he has not commented on the expansive evidentiary basis on which the Trial Chamber relied to conclude that Croatia exercised effective -- sorry, overall control, and so I won't make any specific submissions on that, but I am available to assist Your Honours if you have any specific points you with like me to address. Thank you. That concludes the Prosecution's submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then call Mr. Cerkez's Defence for reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I will first briefly, and very briefly, reply on yesterday's and today's argument of the Prosecution, and then my counsel will wrap up regarding joint criminal enterprise or better to say argument of the Prosecution which now changes the approach taken in trial. But I will continue in Croatian language. It is much easier for me, with your permission. [Interpretation] We heard yesterday a comment to the effect that my submissions on the time elapsed from the invitation to Cerkez to come to command at the time when he was going to his wedding was a instance of my testifying on his behalf. I only referred to two pieces of evidence in the case, and I was only analysing, analysing the existing evidence. I therefore don't believe that I was testifying, because the first piece of evidence shows the time for which the wedding was scheduled, and the second piece of evidence, the 610, shows for when the meeting was scheduled at the headquarters. These exhibits are D94/2, Stipo Ceko testimony, page 2349; the affidavit of Ruza Ceko; the testimony of Drago Pranjes, transcript page 26127; and an indirect piece of evidence, I know it is not a exhibit in this case, but is -- it's a witness C1 in Kupreskic, page 1136. These are pieces of evidence mutually supplement each other and show without a doubt where Cerkez was at the time, but I do abandon this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think it's quite clear for you that the testimony in another case is not part of the evidence before us and therefore it can't be part of our assessment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely true, Your Honour. I reckon that there is always a hypothetical chance that the Appeals Chamber can, proprio motu, take something into consideration, but I know that it is not in evidence. However, the other evidence, Stipo Ceko, Ruza Ceko, and the supporting documents are doubtlessly documents that show that the wedding was scheduled for the time indicated, two months in advance, and therefore Cerkez was not able to go that day to the meeting where allegedly the plan was made. I have to come back to that because the Prosecution has said a lot about this, viewing it from various aspects, and the crucial part of the plan is this meeting. Cerkez, and I have to point this out clearly as we have repeated many times during the trial, had awareness of the military activities in the Lasva Valley and in Vitez on the 16th of April. What knowledge he had, he acquired during the day, and he knew about his part of the task of which he learned early in the morning, and he received part of those orders verbally during the night. Cerkez did not know nor is there any satisfactory evidence that he did, that any crimes were planned or that they were committed. There is no evidence to indicate such a suggestion. However, I have to mention one other thing. According to the judgement, it is indubitable that Cerkez was acquitted of this. He was acquitted of Ahmici. It is another matter that the Trial Chamber found a link, namely that his units were in certain locations, which is a suggestion we deny because we believe there is no satisfactory evidence of that. He was not in this location himself, and we submit that no crimes were committed there. I will now come back to the judgement, paragraph 689. I have referred to this yesterday, and the Prosecution mentioned it in their response. In this part of the judgement, we find subparagraphs (a) to (f), and these form the basis for the later conclusion of the Trial Chamber. I mentioned yesterday, subparagraphs (a) to (c) of this paragraph. The first piece of evidence under (a) was not introduced; it is not part of the evidence. The document under (c) is one whose authenticity we challenged and the Prosecution was unable to authenticate it, and we would like to remind you that this is the only case where we questioned the authenticity of an exhibit. In our appellant's brief, we deal with this matter very extensively, pages 53 to 59. And we did so in the reply to the response by the Prosecution, pages 30 to 38, and page 49. As for document under 689(b), I would like to refer the Appeals Chamber to the finding in the judgement in paragraph 698. This covers a large part of the story, including the value of all these quotations cited under (d), (e), and (f) of the same paragraph. What is this about? The Trial Chamber obviously accepts the Prosecution evidence, the testimony of Josip Zuljevic, correction, Defence arguments, Defence evidence, the testimony of Josip Zuljevic which was quoted yesterday and obviously the Trial Chamber accepted this. In cases where the Trial Chamber did not accept the Defence arguments, it said so explicitly. Josip Zuljevic described in detail the events, and this testimony was completely accepted by the Trial Chamber, and this holds the key to all these notes in 69 -- 689, (a) to (f) on which the Prosecution bids their argument of his knowledge. On the 16th, in the morning chaos reigned. Commander Blaskic demanded from Cerkez, his subordinate, and commander of the only unit which was local to gather all the information available at the time. Zuljevic said explicitly, "We were told to call around, neighbours, friends, duty officers in other units and to gather information in every way possible, and we filed this information with Blaskic." That is clear, and that is confirmed by this paragraph. The Trial Chamber understood this fully, and that is the reason why the judgement does not link Cerkez with Ahmici. From this evidence in paragraph 689, it would seem that Cerkez was in Ahmici. However, the Trial Chamber understood the value and the meaning of this evidence, because you can see that the Trial Chamber does not go any further from the finding it explicitly states. So practically paragraph 689, because of the two documents I referred to yesterday and because of the value of all this other information indicated and the value is clear from the testimony of Josip Zuljevic, is not incriminating for Cerkez, because through the testimony of Zuljevic, from paragraph 689, the value of all this information is clarified. All this information comes from the ground. The village of Donja Veceriska has been 70 per cent done. This is the best information that he was able to gather at the moment somewhere. Or from the other page. No. That is Blaskic speaking. But let me move on. In any case, I believe it was useful to spend some time on this, because this responds to at least half of all the submissions of the Prosecution. The Prosecution further claims that Cerkez was seen on the 15th of April in the evening at the hotel. That was said by Witness AT. We do not question that. We have always admitted that Cerkez came to the hotel, but after the military meeting. AT was staying at the hotel, so he was able to see him, yes. We agree. However, the fact that Witness AT saw him is absolutely not sufficient in the legal sense, in the sense of interpreting the evidence, to claim that he had come for a meeting. The hotel was a point of regular assembly for the troops. It is very far from proving that he attended the meeting, and even less for proving what was discussed at the meeting. Witness AT says himself a bit later that the first orders involving the killing of men were given at the meeting in Nadioci, not earlier at the headquarters. At one point - I don't know if this was by mistake - my learned friend from the Prosecution said they agreed that Cerkez was in Kruscica. Kruscica is a place to the south where he was indeed assigned. And on that day, there was no direct clash between two armies, there was no damage or casualties among the civilians. So if they agree we were in Kruscica and in view of the orders given at the brigade headquarters, then it is obvious that Cerkez could not have been elsewhere in the first days of the conflict. They pointed out at one point paragraph 688, which gives us only a definition of a topic dealt with in the judgement. That is not a finding. Another reference was to paragraph 595 of the judgement. That is the Trial Chamber's finding that the Vitez Brigade was established on the 24th March 1993 and that Cerkez was its commander. Yes, we agree. We admitted that in the pre-trial brief. But the emphasis is on the fact that the brigade was set up only in end March. And in view of the conditions, the living conditions and the general circumstances which tell us a lot about the situation as a whole, it is not to be expected that from the end of March until the 16th of April the brigade was able to organise itself fully. We heard another reference about battalions of this brigade being deployed across villages. That was in 2653 -- that was in Exhibit Z653. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. At least ten witnesses who lived and worked there, including Witness Bertovic, who was a excellent and an impressive witness, told us what this document meant. This document was only for information purposes, Commander Bertovic's own assessment on the potential for mobilisation from a certain village to provide replacement on the front line facing the JNA, the front line he held. Those were not battalion in existence. We spent a awful lot of time in trial proving that, and the Trial Chamber understood this completely. You cannot find any erroneous findings concerning this point. The Prosecution is again, however, coming back to this. This document absolutely does not have the significance given to it by the Prosecution. We need to read witness statements which clearly indicate what this document means, and the Trial Chamber believes them. We can see that from their findings. Furthermore, at one point, the Prosecution refers us to paragraph 596 of the judgement. That again is a claim that the brigade had several battalions. I will not elaborate this whole philosophy again. It is terribly long and full of evidence. I refer you to paragraph 26(a), page 58. In that paragraph, 596, reference is made to Colonel Duncan. However, Duncan says that he assumed there were several brigades, and I remind you Duncan came to Vitez in May when the brigade indeed had more than one battalion. However, here in the testimony that is referred to, Duncan said this was an assumption. We agree, but for the month of May, not April. However, the month of April is the only subject of our discussion here. And secondly, all the charges referred to April. So we can only discuss this within the given time frame. As for the level of organisation of the brigade, I refer you to our appellant's brief, paragraph 26, page 58, which gives us a full analysis and refers you to witnesses Badrov, Sajevic, Ceko and Bertovic. Paragraph 696 contains a finding that our learned friends are using as a argument. Yes, we agree with everything stated there. Witness Buffini was quoted here discussing the work of the so-called Busovaca Joint Commission whose job was to maintain the truce. And that commission was in operation only from the 19th or the 21st of April. Yes, Cerkez took part in the work of that commission. That is the only thing this shows. Cerkez participated in this commission as representative of the HVO in Vitez because he was appointed by Blaskic. We can see this from other documents in greater detail. Franjo Nakic, who was Chief of Staff with Blaskic, and Mario Cerkez were on this commission representing the HVO, depending on the subject discussed. And there is nothing more to it than that. However, the Prosecution is seeking to tell us otherwise. Our colleague Mr. Farrell mentioned also paragraphs -- paragraph 807, subparagraphs (i) to (ii) referring to count 41, the common plan. I believe this is absolutely inappropriate in my opinion. The charges of Cerkez, destruction and plunder, are only limited to April 1993. These two paragraphs refer, however, to incidents in October - Cerkez was never charged with this, nor did he defend himself - and incidents in January. I see absolutely no relevance of this finding to the culpability of my client under count 41. Paragraph 644, Breljas. Breljas is referred to in several places, and he was mentioned again today. This is a matter that needs more time to elaborate, time that I don't have, but I will recall before this Appeals Chamber that we analysed Breljas in great detail and pointed out discrepancies in his testimony, pages 59, 60, 87, in our appellant's brief, plus page 81, footnote 217, and page 87 in footnote 226 in Cerkez's appellant's brief. You will see by referring to these points that this is an absolutely irrelevant argument. Paragraph 643 contains a reference to Colonel Watters, the very beginning of the conflict. It says that Colonel Watters intervened with the commander of the brigade in Vitez but also the commander of the Muslims. What was not said yesterday is this, and I'm quoting the words of the witness, Colonel Watters: "Both sides said the other side attacked them." There is no detrimental finding for Cerkez here. Of course this is how the war started, but there was no attack on the civilians by the HVO. So there is no such finding. This is just a introduction to a new subject. However, having mentioned this witness who was a very valuable one and gave us many curious facts that were assessed as valuable by the Trial Chamber, I would like to refer you to Exhibit D57/1, that is the witness's letter to his father, and I quote his letter in my appellant's brief on page 104, which deals with sentencing. I believe this is the most accurate and from a humane or human point of view, the most beautiful thing ever mentioned in this case. The Prosecution mentioned also Krunoslav Bonic. We have heard so much about him during trial and wasted so much time because this was a claim simply thrown into the courtroom, and the Trial Chamber never mentions him. What is at issue is a set of documents based on which the Prosecution wanted to prove that a group of people who were mentioned as members of the brigade at some time were indeed members of the brigade. We heard a lot of testimony about this and much time was wasted on this. First of all, the Trial Chamber did not accept this logic and did not make any findings based on it. And second, in our response to the appellant's brief of the Prosecution, we deal with it on pages 55 to 73. Today my learned friend Jarvis quoted several findings of the Court speaking about count 41. That was mentioned by Mr. Farrell yesterday as well. However, these are the final findings which have -- which are not based on the factual analysis. Today we've heard about the plan again. I believe there is no need for me to go back to that issue. It's been debated long enough. Now just a few words about the blockade of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, you told us beforehand that you want to give the floor also to your colleague in order to wrap up, and I want to emphasise your time is elapsing in about five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take up just two or three minutes and then I will leave the rest of the allotted time to my colleague, with your leave. Let me just say a few words about the blockade of the bridge based on which Cerkez concluded that -- the Prosecution concluded that Cerkez participated in some kind of a plan. Witness Bertovic testified about that long before Witness AT came, and the OTP asked Witness Bertovic about that alleged blockade. At the time we didn't know why the OTP was asking the witness about that because we didn't hear anything about that earlier and we only learned about that when Witness AT came one or two months later. Witness Bertovic gave a clear explanation. However, Your Honours, if you only look at the map that we have, you will have no need for that explanation. Even had he received such a order, even had the bridge been blockaded, that would still have been pointless because UNPROFOR could have reached that area from two or three directions. So this is a completely senseless story and unfortunately it is very difficult to defend oneself from such stories. Therefore, I ask you to look at the testimony of Witness Bertovic. I will not address the issue of sentencing right now because of the limited time that we have, and I will let my colleague use the remaining time for the issue of joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly in view of the time. I will touch upon the submissions of the OTP given to us today concerning the joint criminal enterprise and the issue of the nature of the armed conflict. As for the first question which is the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise, I would like to say at the outset the following: We do not find the invocation of this doctrine in the indictment. We can also not find it in any of the motions submitted during pre-trial phase. It is not mentioned in any of the testimonies or any of the documents. It is also not mentioned in closing arguments of the OTP. The doctrine was not mentioned in Trial Chamber's judgement either. It is only now in the appeals proceedings that this issue is brought up. The whole story is based on the fact that on the 15th of April, a meeting was held in Blaskic's headquarters where allegedly Mr. Cerkez was also present and where allegedly a joint conclusion was made which was linked to joint criminal enterprise. My learned friend from the OTP said the following: "We have no concrete information regarding that." I'm quoting his words. My learned friend today, Ms. Jarvis, said that logical inference is the only way to prove intent. Based on these words, it is evident that all the OTP's submissions were in fact virtual arguments which have no firm basis. During the proceedings, we never heard from any of the alleged participants of that criminal meeting. During the proceedings, we did not see a single document emerging or emanating from that criminal meeting. We heard testimony of one witness claiming that my client was present at the hotel where the meeting was held, this is all. Based on that, an inference is made that my client was at the meeting where the criminal plan was devised, that he accepted the goals of that plan as his own and therefore was liable for everything that ensued based upon that plan. This reminds me of linking conclusions which are based on a completely wrong premise. What the OTP is doing is actually putting before you, Your Honours, a flawed premise and then making conclusions based on it. We cannot accept that. This is wrong. This has no basis, no support in facts and evidence adduced during trial. We claim, the Defence of Mr. Cerkez claims, that there are no direct and no indirect evidence that any criminal plan was made and that during that process, Mr. Cerkez was present and that he shared the intent of other persons who were allegedly involved in that criminal plan. It is completely clear to me that the theory and doctrine of joint criminal enterprise is a form of criminal liability which in Krstic case, paragraph 601 of the appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber linked to Article 7(1) of the Statute, but if this is a legal issue, I claim that this is also a factual issue. What I'm submitting is that there are no facts that would support this kind of legal conclusion. Therefore, I claim that the participation in joint criminal enterprise has not been proven and, therefore, the crimes that took place in Ahmici and other locations in the Lasva Valley do not emanate from the plan that was allegedly made and with which my client had nothing to do. My learned friend, Ms. Jarvis, spoke today about the discriminatory intent of Mr. Cerkez, and once again she said that the only way to infer this was by using logic. I will now speak about some of the firm evidence that was produced during trial. Numerous witnesses spoke about the views and positions of Mr. Cerkez, about how he respected other people, how he respected diversity and how he respected persons regardless of their political or religious affiliations. We heard no evidence that would show that Mr. Cerkez had any kind of prejudice with respect to anyone; on the contrary. However, what the OTP is offering us now is to make logical inferences, yes, but how can we make such logical inferences if the elements for it are lacking? What we submit is that this thesis is unfounded and that there are absolutely no elements to support it. Just this, your question, Your Honour Judge Schomburg, you asked about the conclusion, about the express orders given by Mr. Cerkez, and I will reply to your question now. There is no such express order, first, because Mr. Cerkez never issued it, and second, because he simply is not the kind of person who would be able to function in that way in that kind of a situation. Mr. Cerkez was part of a military structure; he implemented orders in accordance with the international norms of warfare. I thank you for your attention, and I'm prepared to answer your questions if there should be any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
