utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then we'll get -- we're looking forward for the hard copies presented during your oral submissions. Thank you. And as regards the charts, we come back to this later. So then let's now, without further ado, come to the appeal of the Prosecution, and we expect the submissions by the OTP, hopefully in a very precise and short submission, as promised yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do our best. Your Honour, I'll be addressing on the fourth ground of the Prosecution's appeal on the Prosecution's appeal against Mr. Kordic's sentence. And I won't take very long. What I really want to do is to just flesh out the main bases for our appeal against his sentence, and especially in light of some of the more recent Tribunal case-law that's come out since we filed our appeal. Twenty-five years is a long term of imprisonment, that's for sure. It's a long time in gaol. So why, then, does the Prosecution say that the Trial Chamber imposed a manifestly inadequate sentence and asked the Appeals Chamber to significantly increase it? Simply put, in our submission, the sentence neither reflects the inherent gravity of the crimes or his role in them. The first basis for our appeal, as you know from our Appeal Brief, is that it fails to reflect the magnitude, the scale, the scope, geographically, I'm speaking as well temporally, and the extremely grave nature of these crimes. Yesterday in my response I delved into some of the facts of this case and really this can only provide a snapshot of what can only be described as an overwhelming crime base. In four municipalities in Central Bosnia, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and Vitez, in dozens of towns and villages. We're talking about numerous persecutory acts committed for over a year, in which hundreds of civilians were murdered, thousands had to endure other mistreatments, such as the loss of their homes by being burnt down, the loss of their businesses, their livelihood, the physical and mental sufferings that they endured, having their personal effects stolen, their places of worship burnt down and being rounded up and taken to detention. Just looking alone at Ahmici, we know that this was one of the single worst days in the whole history of the war in the former Yugoslavia. Indeed, the Trial Chamber stated, at paragraph 852 to 853, offences of this level of barbarity could not be more grave and those who participate in them must expect sentences of commensurate severity to mark the outrage of the international community. But in our submission, the sentence doesn't actually reflect an acknowledgment of this principle. The victimisation of the Muslim population could not have been more intense. And I think, particularly important, these crimes were committed against a defenceless population, and as we know from cases such as Kunarac, and indeed recognised in the Banovic sentencing judgement, the vulnerability of the victims must be considered when assessing the gravity. It has to also be recalled that the crimes were carried out as part of a pattern of atrocities, all aimed at the ultimate goal of ethnically cleansing Muslims from the HZ HB. Neither in our opinion, in our submission, does the gravity reflect the merciless modus operandi with which the persecutory acts were committed. Again, the facts are clear from the judgement. The attacks being launched against a defenceless Muslim population in the early hours ensuring that that population would be caught by surprise and unable to defend themselves or flee. And performed in the cruellest manner, including the deliberate burning down of their houses and their looting. We could also say that this is a situation which the Vasiljevic judgement recognised, did increase the gravity of an offence. It was directed -- this approach was directed at minimising the possibilities of an effective defence by the victims, as well as securing the completion of the crimes. We also say another very critical factor was not given due weight, and that is the long phase and the long planning nature which was involved in these large-scale crimes, a principle that was recognised in the Stakic Trial Chamber's judgement at 917. And just finally on this gravity of the underlying crimes, I'd also like to stress that Kordic's familiarity with a lot of the victims, particularly those in Busovaca, must also be something that is properly taken into account and was not so reflected on this occasion. The other prong going to the gravity of these offences relates more to his criminal participation or role in the crimes. And in our submission, the sentence does not properly reflect the form and degree of his participation in these crimes. Yes, time and again the Trial Chamber expressed its view as to how serious these crimes were, and time and again commented on the instrumental role that he played. But when it came down to imposing the sentence, it paid insufficient heed to these matters. And Your Honours need no reminding of the words in the Stakic Trial Chamber's decision at 918: "As with white collar crimes, the perpetrator behind the perpetrator, the perpetrator in white gloves, might deserve a higher penalty than the one who physically participated, depending on the circumstances of the case." In our submission, this is such a case. His role in all of this, ordering, planning, preparing, instigating, sometimes directly, more times indirectly, through this collectivity of criminal action, through a collective of people at which he's in the apex is surely deserving of a much higher sentence. Turning to the second basis for our appeal, and this is that the sentence imposed fails to give sufficient weight to his position and his powers as the highest Bosnian Croat political leader in Central Bosnia at the time, and his abuse of that position. Again, the Trial Chamber did notice, did note, at paragraph 853, that the fact that he's a leader aggravates the offence. But again, in our submission, the actual sentence fails to give due weight to his high position of political leadership in the region as an aggravating factor. Although he travelled under a variety of titles and he had various functions which we could say grew and expanded during the course of the time, during the course of the year, it's clear that we know he was president of the HDZ Busovaca and he was vice-president of the Presidency of the HZ HB throughout this whole period. And he -- and that position was not, in our opinion, reflected in the sentence which was imposed. Likewise, the sentence does not adequately reflect the subsequent abuse of that position. When he contributed to the common criminal design, and thereby, through that common criminal design, planned and instigated and ordered the magnitude of crimes committed upon the Bosnian Muslim civilians in the Lasva Valley and its surrounds, and a number of cases have highlighted that abusive position and authority or influence in order to commit crimes and the betrayal of trust are matters that must be taken into account as aggravating the crime. As for the question of his military role and whether it should aggravate his sentence, this issue as to his military authority has been a source of some ongoing controversy in this case, not just at the trial level but even here during the appeal. Kordic didn't have military authority in the sense of being in a formal chain of command, or even, as the Trial Chamber found, in the sense of having the material ability to prevent or punish. But the Trial Chamber made several very important findings about the true scope of his military position or authority, and I point Your Honours to paragraph 530, where the Trial Chamber found he had a clear role leading the HVO in the fighting. So here his military authority being used in a very direct sense. I also point Your Honours to paragraph 532, in relation to Ahmici barricade incident. Not the subject of a criminal conviction in this matter, but here a finding that the Trial Chamber accepted the Ahmici -- what the Ahmici barricade episode revealed was that he had clear political and military authority by this stage. I also point Your Honours to paragraph 585, in which the Trial Chamber found that he was implicated in the attack in Busovaca as a leader exerting both political and military authority; again, in a very direct sense. And paragraph 642, where Dario Kordic, as a local political leader, was part -- was found by the Trial Chamber to be part of the design or plan for the illegal military attack on the Lasva Valley localities, principally for his role as planner and instigator of it. And finally, I turn Your Honours' attention to the findings in paragraph 767, which were based on evidence given by many of the international witnesses in this case. The Trial Chamber had the evidence of Colonel Stewart, Lieutenant Colonel Watters, Brigadier Duncan, who each spoke about this clear link between the military and the political. Brigadier Duncan stated that while operations were Blaskic's task, planning was Kordic's task, leading the Trial Chamber to make the important finding, in paragraph 767, that these international witnesses' observations "do lend support to the Prosecution case that, as might be expected, the exercise of military power was subject to a political authority." As the Prosecution puts it, Blaskic could not do his job alone without Kordic giving the green light. Now, to pre-empt the appellant's argument, he will argue: Well, he wasn't found to have 7(3) responsibility, so how can this factor be taken into account? In our submission, the question of the basis for his liability should not be confused with these factors, these facts found by the Trial Chamber regarding his clear military authority, which go to aggravate his punishment. The Trial Chamber didn't find he had 7(3) responsibility because they weren't satisfied that he had the material ability to prevent or punish. But that's not why he's being punished here. He's not being punished for his own missions as a leader but for his very positive contributions towards the criminal plan, design, call it an enterprise, through which the crimes were ultimately effected. And again, Your Honours need no reminding about the Stakic Trial Chamber's judgement, but I'd like to read it for the record because I think it so aptly expresses our view on this particular issue. In relation -- when sentencing the accused Mr. Stakic, the Trial Chamber said that it considers the primary aggravating factor in this case is the superior position held by the accused. "Where the factual circumstances are such that a Trial Chamber could reasonably find that specific acts could satisfy 7(1) or 7(3), if a conviction is entered under 7(1) only, the accused's position as a superior, when proved beyond a reasonable doubt, must be taken into account as an aggravating factor. However," and this is the most important point, "the aggravating factor is identical whether the accused is found to have fulfilled the requirements for responsibility under Article 7(3) or is simply proved to have held superior positions." And that, in effect, is a complete mirror of our position on this issue. The final basis for our appeal against Mr. Kordic's sentence is that it differs significantly from the sentence passed by another Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, that is, the sentence on Mr. Blaskic for substantially similar, although not identical, criminal conduct. And the Prosecution recognises that this sentence that Blaskic received of 45 years is pending issuance, delivery of an appeals judgement. But notwithstanding that, and cognisant of the somewhat different forms of liability, Blaskic having at least some 7(3) responsibility for many of the crimes, but the crime base is very, very similar, and it has to be borne in mind that Kordic's liability under 7(1) is for his very linkage to the crimes committed by the HVO and others. And our submission is that notwithstanding the principle of individualisation of sentencing, there shouldn't be substantial inconsistencies in punishing two offenders where the circumstances of the offence and the offenders are sufficiently similar, and especially not in this case, especially not, when the Trial Chamber had found the relationship between Kordic and Blaskic to be joint authorities, and even that Kordic was above Blaskic. It's a complex relationship to put into one irreducible principle, but I think it is well summarised when the Trial Chamber endorsed the Prosecution's comment that Blaskic could not do his job alone without Kordic giving the green light. There are the three main bases for our appeal. I'd also like to make a comment about, more generally speaking, the principles of sentencing when you come to review the sentence. In our submission, for these sorts of crimes, the goals of deterrence and retribution should play a primary role, that is, deterrence in both its general or educative sense, and to express clearly the international community's revulsion and condemnation of these crimes. But also in its individual and suppressive aspect. I'd like to speak about the role of rehabilitation or re-education as a factor in sentencing. My colleague, Mr. Farrell, has already spoken about the approach that this Chamber should take. But if you come to re-sentence Mr. Kordic, our submission is that rehabilitation or re-education of the offender, it is a consideration, but in this particularly grave type of case, retribution and deterrence should outweigh the need for rehabilitation and re-education. But this is not to say that these concepts cannot play a more vital role at a subsequent stage of serving the sentence. We don't resile from our position one bit. These crimes are so grave that they require the imposition of a much higher, significantly higher, sentence. But, if Your Honours are minded to take into account rehabilitation and re-education, the imposition of a very lengthy term with a recommended minimum term, after a set number of years, could be the most effective outcome and one which reflects all the principles and purposes of punishment. And this is an approach which was taken in Tadic and in Stakic. We don't object to the -- excuse me, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we note that the affidavit of Mr. Kordic's wife attesting to the family circumstances of Mr. Kordic is before you, as well as the behaviour report from Mr. Timothy McFadden. As we said, we don't object to the admission or the -- this going before you, but so long as this subject matter is treated in accordance with our position about the respective positions of deterrence and retribution vis-a-vis rehabilitation in a case such as this. And finally, one further matter that I raise as much as a sword in our own appeal as a shield, in relation to his appeal against his sentence. In our response brief, we acknowledged that some of the factors he put forward may, as a matter of law, be mitigating, such as the family circumstances. But in that response brief, our position was that the Trial Chamber made no discernible error in the exercise of its discretion by giving no weight to those factors. And similarly, this should not impede Your Honours from imposing a higher -- a significantly higher sentence. The Celebici Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 847, observed that in certain circumstances, the gravity of the crime may be so great that even following consideration of any mitigating factors, a very severe penalty is nevertheless justified. And we rely on that proposition that where crimes are exceptionally grave, such as this, the -- little or no weight should be given to factors in mitigation. And this proposition has also been subsequently endorsed by the Trial Chamber in Stakic, where, at paragraph 926, the Trial Chamber stated that it considered that the substantial volume of evidence given in favour of the accused, Dr. Stakic's personality and family situation merited consideration, but said, however, this factor will not be given undue weight, given the severity of the crimes. In our submission, that is the exact same approach that should be taken here. That completes my submissions on this ground of appeal, and I'll hand over to my colleague, Mr. Farrell, unless Your Honours have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may begin. The Prosecution's appeal against Mr. Cerkez is twofold. There's an appeal in relation to the acquittal for the crimes committed in Ahmici and the counts for which the Prosecution has sought this Chamber's intervention and the entering of conviction, are set out in paragraph 3.6 of the Prosecution's Appeal Brief. The second aspect of the Prosecution's appeal relates to the sentence imposed on Mr. Cerkez. I just note in relation to the sentence appeal that there are two aspects to it. I won't be making submissions on sentence. The brief is fairly -- it's concise. But the argument is that there is a manifest inadequacy in the sentence of 15 years. The Prosecution's submission is that in light of the role played by Mr. Cerkez, the very prominent one in these -- in this campaign of persecution for which he was found guilty not only to be involved in individual counts but to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise that his sentence should certainly be more than 15 years. The cases subsequent to this one, and there have been a number of sentencing decisions, don't particularly reflect sentencing patterns as of yet before the Tribunal, though there are a few that we'd ask the Court to take into consideration. On a few of the cases where there's been guilty pleas, Banovic, Nikolic, and others, the sentences in those cases where someone has pled guilty for crimes, though of a different nature, crimes of similar magnitude, Mr. Banovic, even though he's involved directly, crimes of a less magnitude in terms of their scope, he received a sentence of 23 years, while Mr. Cerkez, in our submission in a position of authority in a wider range of crimes, only received 15 years. The Vasiljevic judgement is one where the Appeals Chamber has upheld a sentence for 15 years for essentially aiding and abetting in approximately five killings. Mr. Cerkez's sentence is 15 years for something much, much greater than that. The second aspect of the Prosecution's sentence appeal is simply a request that if the Prosecution is successful on its appeal in relation to Ahmici, that the Court increase the sentence. It's not an independent ground of appeal, obviously, because it's not -- can't fault the Chamber for not sentencing for Ahmici if we're not successful on our appeal, but we ask that if we are successful in the Prosecution's appeal regarding Ahmici that you take this into consideration as an independent factor for the increase of his sentence, in light of his liability being changed. If I could now address the Prosecution's appeal in relation to Ahmici. If I could ask Your Honours to please open your judgements to paragraph 831. As you know, a Prosecution appeal or an appeal against an acquittal, an appeal where you attempt to substitute a conviction for the acquittal, requires, in the Prosecution's submission, that we can appeal that under the Statute, but that generally it's limited to the findings of fact. The question is if on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they had applied the law correctly, a conviction can be entered in relation to this ground of appeal that there's an error of fact. That's because this Chamber is in the same position as the Trial Chamber. The facts have been found. There's no need for you to make any factual findings. Based on those facts, if the law was applied correctly, which is a legal de novo function which rests with this Chamber, would the result have been different? There's been a successful appeal against acquittal in the Tadic case, which was an error of fact, not an error of law, but certainly demonstrates the authority of this Chamber to intervene. In paragraph 831, this is the findings as to responsibility, which incorporate the factual findings. Paragraph 831 states: "The Trial Chamber has already held that Cerkez, as commander of the Viteska Brigade, participated in the attacks on Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska, although not in the initial attack on Ahmici." The first sentence indicates that Mr. Cerkez is in a position of authority. He's the commander of that brigade which is engaged in attacks in the municipality and that he has participated in the sense that he is the commander of that brigade. The distinguishing factor between the convictions in the other -- the town or villages in the municipality and the conviction for Ahmici is simply that he was not in the initial attack. That's the finding. That's also the finding in paragraph 703. Paragraph 831 continues: "This was a high point of the campaign of persecution. The accused played his part in that campaign by commanding the troops involved in some of the incidents." That third sentence is clear. He's involved in a joint criminal enterprise and he played his part in that campaign or that enterprise by, through his troops, taking certain steps. His liability is for the joint criminal enterprise of persecution, and the part that he plays, his contribution to that, is the specific acts that they've indicated in Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Donja Veceriska. Paragraph 831 continues: "As such, he was a co-perpetrator, and that he had the necessary mens rea may be inferred also in his case from his part in the campaign." What the Trial Chamber has done here is, in my submission, correctly found as a fact that he was a member, co-perpetrator, in a common purpose to engage in a persecutory campaign, and he played his part, and his part was his direct involvement, and it constituted the contribution. I will take you through other findings in the judgement, but this paragraph alone is sufficient, in my respectful submission, to enter a conviction for the acquittal on Ahmici. He is found as a result to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise, he's found to be contributing to the campaign of persecution, he has played his part, and he has the necessary mens rea. The law on joint criminal enterprise or common purpose was cited by this Trial Chamber, and I don't need to take you to it, but in paragraph 397. It correctly notes that it requires the elements as set out in Tadic and that the participation is, and is limited to, the contribution to the execution of the plan. It cites the law at paragraph 385 to planning, where he intended to participate and committed deliberate acts which contributed directly and substantially to the commission of the crime; that's the Trial Chamber's conclusion regarding planning. And the Trial Chamber sets out the law on aiding and abetting and cites from the Tadic Appeals Chamber, if I recall, that any acts directed to assist, encourage or lend moral support and the support has substantial effect. At paragraph 703, the Court refers to the evidence in relation to the attacks, the attacks on the three areas. It finds that he participated in the attacks. This is for Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Veceriska. And this is inferred from his presence at the military meeting on the 15th of April, 1993, the documentary evidence, and the entries in the duty officer's log. The Court then continues in paragraph 783 and says: "However, there is no evidence which satisfied the Trial Chamber beyond reasonable doubt that he bears any responsibility for the initial attack on Ahmici on 16 April, which was the responsibility of the military police battalion, not under his command." What's the focus here? In my submission, the focus here is on 7(1). The Court is not applying the common purpose doctrine which it cites earlier and for which it finds him guilty at the end of the judgement. The last sentence says that he was not responsible for the initial attack on Ahmici. Well, with respect, and I'll refer some of the facts as found, he actually was and had a role to play in the initial attack. Secondly, he had a role to play in Ahmici in the reports he was receiving and reporting back to Colonel Blaskic. And thirdly, he had a role to play in that his troops went in for the arrest operation at the end of the day. But that doesn't matter. It doesn't matter whether he is or is not directly involved himself in the attack on Ahmici. What matters is that he's a member of a joint criminal enterprise, in which this is part of the plan and which he knowingly contributes by his acts to the overall plan in the municipality. At the end of the day, the Court looks at whether or not the military police battalion are under his command and whether there was any involvement in the brigade in the initial attack, but not, in my respectful submission, on the basis of the liability which they considered and which they cited as the common criminal plan. In paragraph 691, the Trial Chamber concludes, after looking at all the orders which are cited in the page previously, at page 236, I went through those orders yesterday, and in my respectful submission, it is absolutely clear that Mr. Cerkez is involved in the municipality of Vitez in relation to all the attacks taking place in the municipality. Colonel Blaskic's immediate superior and the person responsible for the municipality of Vitez and for the Central Bosnia operative zone is asking the commander of the Vitez Brigade to report back, but more importantly, under subparagraph (C) on page 236, to completely take the villages of Donja Veceriska, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, and Vrhovine." It's not saying, as the appellant is saying: Oh, if you can check with anyone on the ground and see if you can obtain any information that you might be able to get at your disposal, and please funnel it through Mario Cerkez so he can tell me. With respect, that's not the way the military chain of command works and that's not what's being said here. "Completely take the villages." That's an order. The reports back say: "With regard to your subject regarding further combat operations," in other words, the combat operations in the Vitez Brigade, by the Vitez Brigade and in his area of responsibility, and then without going through it, you will see that he's reporting back on the military operations. And I've already mentioned the fact that when he reports back at 2.50 in the afternoon directly to Colonel Blaskic, he talks about the town of Vitez being clean and about the 50 Muslims in the cellar of the brigade police station, and I've already submitted to you and presented yesterday an exhibit from trial that shows that the brigade police station is in Vitez and it's 300 metres from his headquarters. Even if there might have been a doubt, and it's my submission that there cannot be one, with respect to the fact that he was involved in a plan and that the plan arose from the second military meeting, which is listed at 610 of the judgement, that, combined with his involvement, and it's his direct involvement, can leave no doubt that if they would have applied the law on common purpose or planning to the facts before them, they would have convicted. There are numerous findings set out in the judgement regarding the role that was played by the Vitez Brigade. I only want to refer to a few of them. At paragraph 612, there's a discussion of the role to be played by the Vitez Brigade in the common plan. And one of the functions to be performed by the Vitez Brigade, which is accepted by the Trial Chamber, as they accept AT's evidence on the preparation, is that the Vitez Brigade was to prevent UNPROFOR from entering Ahmici. This was before the attack when this decision was made. This was the day before. Now, though you don't need his direct involvement for joint criminal enterprise, the plan included blocking UNPROFOR from getting to Ahmici, in light of Blaskic's orders to kill, to expel, and to burn houses. As a member of the plan, he should be found liable. As a direct participant to ensure the successful operation of the attack on Ahmici by blocking UNPROFOR, it's clear evidence that on that basis alone he is contributing to the attack on Ahmici, either as a joint criminal enterprise or certainly aiding and abetting. The Court notes later on in its judgement, where AT is approached by Pasko Ljubicic, and Pasko Ljubicic blames him - I'm sorry - blames Cerkez and complains about the fact that Cerkez let UNPROFOR through. Pasko Ljubicic is the commander of the military police that was operating in Ahmici, and he complains to Cerkez. And what AT says Cerkez's response is: He doesn't respond I don't have any function to perform, I don't know what you're talking about. He blames it on Bertovic. Bertovic was his deputy commander, of the Vitez Brigade, and he blames the fact that UNPROFOR gets through on his deputy commander. He doesn't deny that that was his role or that there was no responsibility for that. That's according to AT's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to be clear on that, please, to which part of the judgement or evidence before us you guided us just --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course. If I can just find it. I'm sorry. I just recall that ... It's in paragraph 692. And if you look at the beginning of paragraph 692, or I can read out the first. It's a long paragraph with a number of subparagraphs. And the beginning of 692 says: "The Prosecution called evidence which demonstrated Mr. Cerkez's reaction to these events." And then under (d), it refers to his response when Pasko Ljubicic complains about UNPROFOR being allowed into Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, in which Cerkez said it was not his fault but Bertovic's. Or he goes on and says the explanation was that UNPROFOR went around the barricade. So there was, if you accept AT's evidence, of course, and the Trial Chamber has found that AT's evidence with respect to the preparation was credible, you have the involvement, first of all, the agreement prior to the attack, the assignment of a task prior to the attack, the function in relation to Ahmici, and then the explanation that UNPROFOR was able to get around the barricade. There's ample evidence of the coordinated campaign, coordinated military campaign which results in the persecution. There's the substantial evidence of the fact that the attacks take place at around 5.30 until 6.00 in the morning, in a number of places, Vitez, Stari Vitez, Kruscica, Donja Veceriska, Ahmici. There's the evidence as to the crimes that were committed in each one of these places, all pointing to the fact that there was a coordinated persecutory campaign by, at a minimum, the four members who were at the meeting on April 15th, those four members, as you recall, are Pasko Ljubicic, who is in Ahmici, Mr. Cerkez, AT says Mr. Grubesic was there, and you will remember Mr. Grubesic's role is to launch the initial artillery shell into Ahmici which was to commence the attack, and AT's evidence also indicated that Mr. Grubesic, as the commander of the Busovaca Brigade, was to block UNPROFOR if they came from the direction of Busovaca. I also note that at the end of the day, as I've indicated before - I think it's in the war diary, 1755, and the Trial Chamber refers to it - there is reference to the fact that -- I'll just refer to it. If you'll give me one moment. It's in paragraph 656, referred to by the Trial Chamber in reliance on their findings. And at 1755 on the 16th of April, 1993, it indicates that there's information recorded in the logbook and listed as Dusko, Cerkez, and Pasko. Dusko, is, in the Prosecution's submission, Grubesic, who AT said was in the meeting on the 15th, whose role was to block the Kaonik-Busovaca road and who was in charge of the artillery from Hrasno hill. Cerkez, we know, and Pasko, in the Prosecution's submission, is Pasko Ljubicic. And then it indicates Donja Veceriska, Ahmici, the places. Then it says the HVO is carrying out arresting people. In the Prosecution's submission, that's the Viteska Brigade. The Trial Chamber found that the evidence clearly points to organised HVO attacks in these areas. The Trial Chamber found that the Viteska Brigade was in the thick of the fighting and that Mario Cerkez was in command of that brigade. The Trial Chamber found that there is clear evidence that Mario Cerkez, as commander of the Viteska Brigade, participated in the attacks on Vitez, Stari Vitez, and Veceriska. It finds that his participation was during the high point of the campaign of persecution and that he played his role and contributed to the campaign by commanding his troops in these incidents. The Trial Chamber found that he was at the military meeting on April the 15th, in which Blaskic gave the assignments. The Trial Chamber found that he was part of a coordinated attack. The Trial Chamber relied on the reports by which Blaskic is asking for a report in the municipality of Vitez, including Ahmici. The Trial Chamber finds that in the cases where Mr. Cerkez participated in the attacks as commander of the Viteska Brigade, he committed those with the intent to commit the crimes as a co-perpetrator in the campaign. That brings me back to paragraph 831. Understanding the judgement, in light of the facts that I've just mentioned, the Trial Chamber then finds that he "participated in the attacks during the high point of the campaign as a co-perpetrator to the common purpose, playing his part in that campaign by commanding troops with the necessary mens rea." With respect, based on those findings and a proper application of either planning or joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber erred and should have entered a conviction for Ahmici. Those are the submissions of the Prosecution. There's a second aspect in our brief regarding evidence that was not referred to but we rely on it, it's in the brief, but I will not make any submissions on it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.text: I had not really prepared, but I think I can handle it. Just give me just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can do it, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The first matter I would like to say is that there's been a lot of repetition, which, in a way, is unavoidable, because, on the other hand, the OTP, yesterday and this morning, gave its response to the appeal of Mr. Cerkez, and then just now they presented their views concerning the acquittal of Mr. Cerkez on the Ahmici count. And the facts are what is important here. Both of these issues boil down to the question whether the facts have been established accurately; second, whether they have been interpreted appropriately; and third, what inferences can be made based on those facts. You've already heard what our position is concerning the key evidence that was used to find Cerkez criminally liable for the participation of his unit in the events in Donja Veceriska and the other location. So the focus, again, is the plan. And once again, we come back to Witness AT. On the one hand, we have hearsay evidence of that witness about the infamous meeting. The witness claims that the meeting was held. He doesn't know what has been agreed at the meeting, so he doesn't know, we don't know, whether there was a plan and what kind of a plan. However, what the witness does know, and what he testified to, is that the killings were mentioned for the first time in the meeting that was held later in Nadioci, the meeting that was attended only by the military police. So how does that implicate Cerkez in the sense that he knew about the plan? There is no evidence. There are no findings to support that Cerkez had anything to do with the military police, so that he could have learned about it from them. It is clear that after that infamous military meeting, military police left the headquarters of Blaskic, the hotel, and went to Nadioci, to the Bungalow there, to further develop their plan for the operation. There is no evidence pointing to the fact that Cerkez could have known anything about that, being involved in that. Second, credibility of that witness. Your Honour, I have to reiterate once again that this is a witness who is completely not credible. He's a convicted murderer and a liar, and there are documents which prove that. We do not have any witnesses who -- I'm sorry. Witness AT states that there was a person who attended the meeting, Mr. Grubesic; however, when Mr. Grubesic came here to testify, he said that he did not attend the meeting. As for the claim that Cerkez attended the meeting, we should look at Exhibit D161. This exhibit proves that Cerkez did not attend the meeting. Therefore, it is clear, based on all of the evidence, that Cerkez did not attend the meeting. Second, even had he attended the meeting, there is absolutely no evidence, no evidence whatsoever, as to what kind of a criminal plan was made at the meeting. We agree that some kind of a military plan was made, and how do we know about that? We know that based on those four orders that I've spoken to you about, those orders are D160/2, D343/1 through 6, 7, and 8. So, yes, there was a military plan; however, that was a legitimate, lawful military plan. The other issue is that part of that legitimate military plan was transformed into something else in Ahmici, and it was transformed into criminal conduct. Why this happened, we don't know. There is ample evidence to show that the 4th Battalion was sent to that place and that that unit did more than it was authorised to do based on the order. As for other units, I wouldn't say that other units overstepped their scope of authority. The area of responsibility of my client, for which my client is responsible, is Kruscica alone, which is to the south of Ahmici. We heard many witnesses, very credible witnesses, testify to the fact that nothing whatsoever happened in Kruscica. The other issue that the OTP spoke about is that Mr. Cerkez received -- assisted in compiling and gathering information. Now, this assistance of Mr. Cerkez during the 16th of April, when he truly was gathering information, or his people, pursuant to his orders, were gathering information from this entire chaotic region and reporting this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information back to Blaskic, which, in a military structure, is a situation where a subordinate reports back to his superior, and the information required by the superior. We have clear testimony of witnesses supporting this. One of them is Witness Zuljevic, which is mentioned in paragraph 698 of the judgement. Therefore, they were gathering information. Now, whether, after the criminal plan was allegedly made, and after the crimes in Ahmici were committed, we have now to establish whether the assistance provided by Cerkez after the fact, after the crime has been committed, can be considered a criminal conduct of co-perpetration or aiding and abetting. [In English] Your Honour, if you could instruct me how much time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All in all you have one and a half hour, and it's now ten minutes to go before the break, and then we'll restart one hour later, and then you have one hour and 10 minutes at your disposal, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I will use this time until the break, and then my counsel will use some time, if necessary. [Interpretation] The next issue that has been revisited today is the fact that the OTP referred us again to paragraph 689(c). However, this time the OTP mistakenly referred you to page 236, which is the same exhibit that I mentioned many times, Exhibit Z692.3. And we challenge the authenticity of this exhibit. I will state once again that over 4.600 documents were introduced into evidence in this trial. Our Defence did not challenge the authenticity of any other document but that one. I would like to bring to your attention, Your Honours, that there are about 70 orders of Blaskic in evidence in this case. All of his orders, of the same character as this order, 692.3, ordering military action, are very precise and very detailed. This unfortunate order, 692.3, I would like to locate it now. Here it is. Could we please place it on the ELMO. Could I have the assistance of the usher, please. Therefore, a brief order, like the one we see now, ordering certain military action, did not come out of Blaskic's headquarters. We saw about 70 orders of Blaskic introduced into evidence in this case, and we haven't seen a single one resembling this one. Second, comparing this order to the other 70 orders, comparing its appearance, its typeset, and so on, we can see that it is completely different. Third: In the military sense, it is simply impossible. It would be senseless to order something like this. They are here ordering to the Vitez Brigade to go to Sivrino Selo. First of all, nowhere in trial was it mentioned, was it indicated in any document, in any testimony, that the HVO had attempted to take Sivrino Selo. I am hereby urging the Prosecution to search all of their databases to see if they can locate this fact. This is impossible because this location was a stronghold of the other army, and the HVO wouldn't have dreamed of trying to take it. Second, this order was issued at 10.30, allegedly, at 10.30. As you saw on the map, Ahmici is an area encompassing Santici, Pirici, Nadioci and so on. From a military point of view, and this is a military case, Your Honour, it would be completely senseless. It would be analogous to me sending my forces to occupy Netherlands. This order does not describe the assignment, the task given to the units. No other order of Blaskic is so lacking in detail and precision. I don't think we will need the ELMO any more. Thank you. Fourth: This order was shown by the OTP to two witnesses: Stipo Ceko and Bertovic, when they testified here, and that was the first time the Defence saw that order. As I've said to you -- I'm a bit unprepared now, so I cannot tell you about the exact reference in the transcript. However, you can see it in our brief. Bertovic was very firm, gave a very assured evaluation of that document, as did another witness, witness Zuljevic. I've said a wrong name just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Am I correct that you are referring to footnote 1393 on this certain document, where it reads of this order: "Anto Bertovic said in re-examination that it would require three strong battalions to carry it out"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And then further Bertovic explained this. Basically, if I recall that correctly, he was surprised by the document. The other witness as well. [Interpretation] Therefore, in my view, due to questionable authenticity of this document, it should be assigned no significance. Even if we were to consider this document as authentic, it still does not link Cerkez to any plan, because it is obvious that plan was devised prior to the drafting of this document. Another matter that I consider to be important is this: The OTP does a very similar thing as the Trial Chamber. They are basically making their inferences based on the events that transpired on the following day, which means that they think that every plan was implemented the way it was designed. I don't think that I need to point out to you how ridiculous this view is, because this morning, what I planned this morning, did not really unfold the way I planned it. This happens to all of us. So how can we conclude that on the 16th of April, things transpired exactly as they had been planned, and we don't know how they had been planned; however, we know that they had been planned because of the way events unfolded? I don't think that this is a proper conclusion. I think that in order to conclude that there had been a plan, we need to have convincing evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- for having a break? The hearing stays adjourned until one hour and 30 minutes, half past 1.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. For the housekeeping, first of all, the Chamber decided, based on the submissions by the Prosecution, that the Chamber will accept hard copies of the charts prepared by the Kordic Defence. However, this is not evidence. We don't attach any probative value to this, and we are fully aware of the submission by the Prosecution that it does not accurately reflect the judgement. It's only a kind of assistance of recalling points made by the party. So therefore, we need not attach any exhibit number, and it's for the Kordic Defence to distribute these charts. Thank you. And now we can continue, for the next 70 minutes, one hour and ten minutes, with the Cerkez Defence responding to the Prosecution. Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I do hope that we will be done before -- in shorter time than allocated to us. [Interpretation] In fact, I can tell you, in brief, that I will need approximately ten minutes to cover a few minor points in response to the arguments of the Prosecution. Then my colleague Mr. Mikulicic will make a few points in connection with the plan, in connection with the joint criminal enterprise and intent. After this, I will speak briefly about sentencing. In connection with document Z6923, which I have spoken about extensively, I wish to make just two more points in connection with this document. I wish to remind the Chamber that this document, as a exhibit, was adduced as a exhibit after having travelled for about six years from Bosnia to the Zagreb archives. There are no facts and there is no knowledge as to where these HVO archives were during these six years. Of course, we all believe that various intelligence services dealt with those archives, but we have no evidence to support this. The fact is, however, that these documents turned up in Zagreb in the year 2000, when the government of Croatia, in January 2000, opened up the archives to the Office of the Prosecutor, literally speaking opened, because for a while the investigators of the OTP had access to these archives in the HIS offices - this is one of the intelligence services of Croatia - after which the Croatian government decided to remove the confidentiality of all these documents and to entrust them to the national archives, where the Prosecution continued its search of the documents, as did the investigators of the Defence. However, this was a difficult task for all of us. It was a bit like playing bingo, because the archive had not been properly ordered and classified, so that in the first box you might find a document in favour of the Defence or the Prosecution, or you might go through 120 boxes without finding anything. According to some information, this archive was four kilometres long. In any case, this document arrived from Zagreb - this we know - and the Prosecution called a witness, an analyst, Mr. Prelec, who spoke of the origin of this document, and we do not challenge that this document was found in the Zagreb archive. However, this witness confirmed two points: First, that he knew nothing of what happened to this document before it turned up in the Zagreb archives, and he could not testify to its authenticity; and secondly, this witness confirmed something that has an effect on the entire procedure, and that is that most of the documents found there by the Prosecution concerning the Vitez Brigade had been in the possession of the Prosecution by May 2000, and yet these documents were not disclosed to us. So we are bringing up the equality of arms here. This document was shown to two of our witnesses, first to Witness Bertovic, before the testimony of AT, and Bertovic explained this document. I will not speak any further about this document, but we abide by our assertion that this document is not authentic. We raised this objection during the trial itself, and along with these arguments, viewed analytically, as every Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber should, this document does not adhere to the standard and is, therefore, suspect. The second matter I wish to raise is that the OTP used a quote from paragraph 612 of the judgement about the task of the Vitez Brigade to prevent UNPROFOR from reaching Ahmici or other places. In our response, I spoke briefly about this, but I now have to reiterate. This was, in fact, stated by Witness AT. Your Honours know that we consider this witness not credible, except insofar as he may have been in Ahmici, but the rest of his testimony is not credible. This story was not mentioned by any other witness. This was the only time we heard it. Secondly, this statement is totally illogical and impossible. That is to say, in view of the location of the roads and the other elements in Vitez, there is no way that the Vitez Brigade could have blocked the access of anyone to Ahmici or any other location, because UNPROFOR had two large bases, one at the eastern side and the other one at the western side of the town, so that even had a barricade been set up, and Witness Bertovic denied it firmly, and it was stated that it was Bertovic who held that barricade near the Impregnacija. So this, in fact, does not hold water. It is so illogical that I can find no words to describe it. Let me mention that my learned friend, in connection with Bertovic, who I believe was an impressive witness, as can be seen from the judgement in several places, my learned friend said that Bertovic was Cerkez's deputy, when in fact there is no doubt, from a large amount of evidence, that Bertovic was actually the commander of a battalion in the Vitez Brigade, and at that time, in April, it was the only battalion in the Vitez Brigade, and he testified to this. I have now come to a further argument, which was indirectly mentioned today through quoting a paragraph from the judgement and was put on the ELMO yesterday. This is document Z653. And yesterday I mentioned that this document was on the ELMO countless times during the Trial Chamber -- during the trial, and the Chamber did not draw any conclusions from it. Bertovic testified about this document. I think he said that he had drawn it up. But in any case, this document was, in fact, an analysis of the mobilisation potential for the call-up of soldiers, of conscripts, into the shifts that went to the defence line facing the army of the Bosnian Serbs. And this was well known, that the HVO used the principle of shifts to cover this area of defence against the VRS. Bertovic, who was a major in the brigade, testified about the way manpower levels were brought up to level in the shifts, and he had to convince his commander, Cerkez, about the potential that he had at his disposal, in theory, and, as he testified, it was always a problem for him to put together a shift of 65 or 70 men, which was the number he needed. Secondly, the Vitez Brigade has a number of documents concerning this, up to this conflict, as part of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, and then later on, when it was established as the Vitez Brigade, its only task was to maintain the lines facing the VRS. It was never either organised or trained or in any way prepared for fighting in a built-up area. I would also like to say that, as I said before the break, there is no other piece of evidence to show that Sivrino Selo was a target of the HVO in any way. My learned friend, during the break, reminded me that AT stated this, that the Vitez Brigade had such aspirations or that the military police was in Sivrino Selo. In any case, Sivrino Selo was mentioned as a location of HVO activity. To this, I have to respond. I'm correcting myself now. It was mentioned apart from order 693. However, this was stated by a witness whose testimony we challenge. We challenge its credibility. And secondly, it was the only such piece of information. And in any case, nothing actually happened in Sivrino Selo, however, that may be, and it was not the scene of any crime. This was, however, a occasion for the Prosecution and the judgement to construct conclusions to the effect that the Vitez Brigade was present in various locations, including even Sivrino Selo, overlooking Ahmici. However, there is only one piece of evidence to show this, and Witness AT, but we find that there are insufficient grounds for this conclusion. Further, I think that this is an appropriate place, in view of the Prosecution argument about the legal status of Cerkez in connection with the crime in Ahmici. I will draw attention to the constantly shifting charge against Cerkez in relation to the crime in Ahmici. I wish to say that the Prosecution is continuing to do this during the appeal proceedings, and this is making it much more difficult for Cerkez to defend himself against this charge. This is the way it has been in this case from the first day. My colleague Mr. Sayers mentioned the moving-target theory, and this is one example of it. The situation was as follows: In the amended indictment, the Prosecution states that Cerkez was directly involved in the crime in Ahmici. This follows from counts 5 and 6, 4 to 12, 40 to 42, and 42 to 44. In his opening statement at the start of trial, the Prosecutor, pages 95, 96, and 31 of the trial transcript, alleged two things. First, they said that the HVO perpetrated the crime in Ahmici, and two units were specifically mentioned by name, but the Vitez Brigade was not specifically mentioned. So the Vitez Brigade was not included in this part of the opening statement when the Prosecution was putting forward its case and when we began to understand what charges we had to defend against, in view of the vague indictment. Further, during the Prosecutor's case in chief, the Prosecutor continued attempting to prove that the Vitez Brigade participated directly in the operations of the 16th of April in Ahmici and offered a quantity of evidence to support this. Just before the end of the Defence case in chief, on the 12th of October, 2000, page 26518 of the transcript forward, there are two statements I wish to draw attention to. I will read the quotations. [In English] "Cerkez was involved with his men in part of an overall plan, but was not the particular brigade going in first thing in the morning to kill all the people in Ahmici." [Interpretation] And secondly: [In English] "Once dirty work is done, it may be that the Viteska Brigade was brought in to secure positions, no incompatibility at all." Let me mention this this was stated on the 12th of October, on the eve of the testimony of AT. Why? In order to make this witness credible. So suddenly the Prosecution case has changed. In the rebuttal case, the Prosecution did not change its arguments, so we assume it abided by what was just stated. And in the closing brief, the same standpoint was retained, more or less, because it was said that the Vitez Brigade, under Cerkez's command, was not involved in the operation in Ahmici, but he, Cerkez, was part of the plan and played a role. That's paragraph 252 of the closing brief of the Office of the Prosecutor. And now we come to the appeal. In the Prosecution appeal, they go back to square one and they say that the Vitez Brigade directly participated in the crimes in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. Of course, we have always had the same defence, more or less, but this has become very difficult for us, because every time there is a different description of the crime, and at one point some pieces of evidence may seem irrelevant to us, in view of the Prosecution case, and then suddenly they become very important. But we did not challenge those pieces of evidence on time because we weren't prepared to do so. Responding to the Prosecution arguments about Cerkez's alleged participation in the crimes in Ahmici, I suggest that this ground of appeal be rejected and that its merits be not discussed at all, because just before the end of the trial, the Prosecution explicitly abandoned the thesis that Cerkez's unit was in Ahmici. According to continental law, I can only understand this as a change of the indictment, an amendment of the indictment. And in essence, it was an amendment of the indictment, because just before the end of the trial, on the 12th of October, the Prosecution shifted its argument that the Vitez Brigade had been in Ahmici, only to go back on this at the start of the appeal. Therefore, we submit that the Appeals Chamber should consider dismissing this ground of appeal without discussing its merits at all. I now wish to give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, and then after he has spoken, I will speak for a further five minutes on sentencing, if there are no questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this courtroom, above all of us, there is a plan looming above our heads, and it is from this plan that all the evils emanate for which we are all sitting here anyway. Now, this reminds me a little bit of a thesis whereby everything is God's will around us, although we can't see it, although it has not actually been established and proved, but it is there looming above us somewhere. But let's return to some facts. The Prosecution claims that our client, our defendant, was part of a criminal enterprise which was based and founded with the objective of persecuting the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the plan was made more concrete at that meeting of the 15th of April, 1993, that questionable meeting at the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic. We have already heard arguments as to the evidence that indicates that, one point, that the meeting was held at all; two, who was present at that meeting; and three, what the conclusions and decisions at the meeting were. I say with full responsibility once more that in the presentation of evidence, not a single shred of evidence or proof was put forward which would, without any doubt, speak to the fact that -- or, rather, what the subject of the meeting was, who it was who attended that meeting, and what kind of decision was made at the meeting. Let me go back to the Krnojelac judgement for a moment, in which a standard was set, or rather, what the Prosecution had to prove, the rationale for it to be assumed that this type of crime and liability existed. The conditions are, of course, cumulative. The Prosecution has to prove what plan there was, what the purpose of the plan was. It must identify the other participants or, rather, perpetrators, and it must prove a concrete category of crime for which the person accused is being charged. I should like to remind you here of the standard used in the Krstic judgement as well, where it is expressly stated that the mere fact that somebody was present in a locality is not sufficient for one to conclude on that person's liability and that that person should be held responsible. In his introduction, my learned colleague of the Prosecution refers to paragraphs 703 and 831 of the judgement, in which the Trial Chamber, in fact, claims that it cannot conclude beyond reasonable doubt as to the responsibility of our defendant with respect to the crimes in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ahmici, and because of that, it finds our client not guilty on that count; it acquits him. Now, what does my learned colleague do? He reinterprets this position from the judgement by the Trial Chamber, and he does so in the following way: He draws the reverse conclusion and, in fact, establishes the existence of a plan and, once again, accountability and responsibility of that on the part of my client. If we look at the initial indictment, the original indictment, we will see that the indictment deals with various concepts, such as aiding and abetting in the perpetration of a crime, but not in a single section is this category of accountability within the framework of a joint enterprise mentioned. The judgement itself in paragraph 397, for example, refers to the doctrine of the common purpose and the various forms of aiding and abetting within that context. These are not categories which mean the same thing and are of the same order. They are not identical. Here I should like to refer to the Blaskic judgement, paragraph 288, where it is stated that a distinction must be made between aiding and abetting and a common purpose or joint plan. I should once again like to refer to the Krnojelac judgement dated the 15th of March, 1992, paragraph 75, in fact, of that judgement, by states the following: "An individual who just aids and abets the perpetrator must be conscious of his intention for a crime to have taken place, whereas the participant in a common enterprise or according to the common purpose doctrine, must share intent. That is to say, he must share the intent of the prime perpetrator or as it is said in the original, the principal offender." Therefore, I claim, I put it to you that there is no evidence and proof in this trial which would lead us to conclude, A, that our defendant was present at the meeting at all where this common plan was established; and B, that there is no proof or evidence that any such plan existed, that any plan was decided upon; and C, that there is no evidence or proof that my defendant, even if he was at the meeting and if a joint plan was devised, that he shared intent with the rest of the participants. It is true that when it comes to the existence of a plan of this kind, we can make an opposite conclusion. We can conclude vice versa through various forms of perpetration of crimes, various crimes committed, in fact, which become a standard method of committing those acts. However, let us take a look at what happened in our case. The focal point is, of course, the crime in Ahmici, or rather, the central factual point, and, without doubt, a war crime had been committed, where a military operation escalated in such a way that innocent civilians were killed, women and children, in the basements of their houses, where they had hidden and taken shelter during the fighting and the battles and military operations that were going on all around. This form, or rather, these consequences, are not to be found in a single other event in the Lasva River Valley. Ahmici is truly an isolated case. They are a very unfortunate incident, a terrible war crime, for which, without any doubt at all, the perpetrators must receive their due sentence and be punished, but among them is not my defendant. You have heard the arguments put forward about where the tempore acti lies and where my defendant was, where he was physically present. You have heard arguments put forward which the Defence used to refute the position taken by the Prosecution with respect to the existence of a common enterprise or common crime and common purpose doctrine, and it is up to you, Your Honours, to reach your own decisions. I consider that the Trial Chamber, in this part, when it came to responsibility for the crimes in Ahmici, made the right decision and that there are no relevant arguments which would indicate that you should draw different conclusions. And I will complete my part of the response here to the Prosecutor's appeal. If there are any questions, I shall be happy to answer them, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no questions. Thank you for your submission. Then I take that it that Mr. Kovacic wants to finalise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very, very brief. First I would -- sorry. I will speak Croatian. It's easier. [Interpretation] First of all, for the record, I would like to say that we fully stand by our written appeal, what we set out in writing, especially with regard to sentencing, and we have nothing to add on that score. In that respect - and we discussed this earlier on - we filed a brief of the 4th of May, and we personally consider that this is a good development in our proceedings and practice because, quite obviously, one of the criteria in weighing up the sentencing must be individualisation of the sentencing and punishment. So I wish to state loud and clear that we fully agree, more or less, with standard court practice, especially where it is claimed that a sentence is weighed up once all the elements of prevention are taken into account, accountability, and the severity of the crime committed, and after that, the individualisation of the sentence is resorted to, once all the other elements have been taken into consideration, and those other elements are mitigating elements or the reverse, aggravating. So we agree with these basic principles and we trust that the Appeals Chamber will try and strike the right balance. Of course, it is not an easy thing to do. Now, in our motion or brief of the 4th of May, we wanted, in fact, to focus on two aspects. One is what the Pre-Appeals Judge gave us the opportunity of doing, that is, presenting personal data and family data about our defendant. And I must say, I took this in a little broader sense, because I feel that every individual is the product of his background and origins, and so it was along these lines that I made free to add certain elements which I think speak to the character of the accused. We have heard the position of the Prosecution on that score. Nonetheless, I do think that these are elements that the Appeals Chamber must have before them so that you can make the right decision, not only with respect to mitigating circumstances but also the scope our client has to improve. And in modern criminology [as interpreted], the aspect of reform is gaining in importance. I'm not going to look into the literature at this point. I don't think that is necessary. But, for the record, it says "modern criminology." I said "modern penology." So may that be put right, please. Also, that reminds of conclusion 470 of the judgement, and I'd like to draw the Court's attention to this, in which certain facts about the accused were set out, and, among other things, it says that many Prosecution witnesses and a number of Defence witnesses spoke positively about the defendant with respect to the absence of prejudice or bias. And this section mentions Colonel Stewart in particular, a Prosecution witness, who gave a positive assessment of the accused's character and said that he was an apparently decent and honourable man, referring to Cerkez. I don't want to make any capital out of this, but I would like to indicate for Your Honours point 21 of the brief. And in Cerkez's wish to show that he has reformed and in his wish to contribute to having the truth prevail about the sad events that took place in the Lasva River Valley, he offered us, or rather, offered the Prosecution that he be a witness in the Hadzihasanovic trial, because he read about certain events in that indictment which he feels he can testify about, and he also offered to give certain expertise to the Prosecution in the legal understanding of documents and placing certain events within the context of the overall situation. This proposal on his part was, unfortunately, rejected. And once again, in Cerkez's brief with respect to his conduct, it shows that he is a individual who is ready to respect the law and rules and regulations and conventions which apply to him and around him, to the world around him, and this is being borne out today with the letter by the Detention Unit's head, and I think it is a valuable contribution to that. I don't think it was a letter written routinely. I think it was written very well. Every word was well-balanced, and I must also say that it is well known that the head of the UN Detention Unit, Mr. McFadden himself is a highly respected and recognised expert in the field of penology today, and Cerkez knows him personally, he has known him for seven years personally. Let me also remind you that Mr. Cerkez reached the Detention Unit at a time when it was a relatively small circle of accused, when there were not many accused there, and when the administration of the Detention Unit had ample opportunity to get to know each of the inmates very well and to understand them. Of course the situation today is somewhat different because it has burgeoned and grown in size. I hope that with having said those main points that I have said everything, but just allow me a few more words and a few more minutes of your time if I may to say the following: In view of the multitude of arguments put forward in this case, especially legal arguments, I should like to ask the Chamber to bear in mind in conformity with the beneficium cohesionis which in the Kupreskic appeal was recognised, and when I say that I mean that Kordic's Defence has presented several important points with respect to legal qualifications and that there is no collision among our defence cases and Defence positions and that everything that was put forward to the advantage of the accused, Mr. Kordic, can be used for the defence of Mr. Cerkez as well, if you accept the basic premises, of course. And with respect to sentencing, a now more words. I propose that the Court should weigh up the sentence and sentence our accused according to whatever they have heard, and I'm sure that points 35 and 44 of the counts in the indictment will be dropped, and I am sure that the double culpability pursuant to Article 7(1) and 7(3) will be dropped in all counts of the indictment from 3 to 44, and I propose that the Court, with respect to this substantially reduced accountability, that this should be reflected in the sentence and the sentence reduced as well. Of course, if we have succeeded in putting forth our appeals case, we would be happy to see the overall sentence lowered as well. Thank you and I am prepared to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no questions. Thank you. Then we can continue immediately with the response by the Kordic team. And as allocated previously, you have no doubt 30 minutes to go for your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I might confess that is a considerable relief to find out, Your Honour. Let me start by saying that we believe that the appropriate approach to take at this stage is not to dwell in the realm of generality but to focus on really four things: What is the standard of review? What are the Trial Chamber's findings? What is the evidence? And what were the Trial Chamber's conclusions? And from all of that, the question has to be asked whether the Trial Chamber has committed error in assessing a extremely severe 25-year sentence. Our respectful submission is there was no error. The burden is on the Prosecution to show a discernible error in the exercise of the Trial Chamber's sentencing discretion. And our respectful submission is it has not even come close to doing so. It must be remembered that Mr. Kordic was acquitted on all of the Article 7(3) charges. This was a full-throttle Article 7(3) case, and no effort was spared in an attempt to prove that Kordic wielded military powers. The conclusion of the Trial Chamber was that he did not. One of the principal military witnesses from the Prosecution, Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, the BritBat commander of the Vitez area, specifically stated that he did not think Kordic had personally been involved in war crimes. The Trial Chamber disagreed. Yet nonetheless, the Prosecution now asks the Appeals Chamber to increase the sentence because of Kordic's asserted position, powers, and responsibilities. The submission is that effectively, he did have the powers of a military commander. The Trial Chamber, on the other hand, found that this was not a commander. Mr. Kordic was not a superior. I've been before, I've gone over this recitation before. I'm not going to repeat everything, but most important thing is that the Trial Chamber concluded that he was a regional political leader. He lacked effective military control over HVO forces. He was not in the highest echelons of leadership of the Bosnian Croat political institutions. He did not conceive of this campaign of persecution that the Trial Chamber found, nor was he the architect of it, nor was he a prime mover in it. The standard of review as I have put on the screen here is uncontroversial. It's the obligation of the appellant to demonstrate a discernible error and as long as the Trial Chamber keeps within proper limits the Appeals Chamber will not intervene. It's the obligation of Trial Chambers to individualise the penalties that are assessed in the cases before them, and that's a obligation imposed by Article 24(2), given that the decision is, in a particular case, discretionary and it turns on the circumstances of a particular case. That's why it's not useful particularly to compare sentences between accused in different cases, and that's the current status of the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence. The burden of proof is absolutely upon the appellant to demonstrate how the Trial Chamber has ventured outside its discretionary framework. So that's what the -- the Prosecution has to prove in this case. Its first argument, the Trial Chamber somehow committed a error in failing to take into account properly the gravity of the offences. Yet the two paragraphs shown on the screen here show that that's precisely what the Trial Chamber did do. The starting point for the consideration of sentence is the gravity of the offence, and the most important consideration in sentencing is the gravity of the offence. So it's a uncomfortable position for the Prosecution to advance here to say that the Trial Chamber failed properly to take into account the very factors that the Trial Chamber said it took into account. The next position is that the Trial Chamber somehow failed to take -- to give due weight as a aggravating factor, and I emphasise that, to Kordic's positions, powers, and responsibilities. The thesis seems to be that Kordic had a high position of political leadership, but it's never really specified what that position was; that he had a role in military matters, again, it's never specified what that role was; that he carried out attacks and exerted military authority; that he had a very important position. Once again, Your Honours, dwelling in the realm of generality. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber committed error in failing to give due weight to Kordic's position as a political leader, but look at paragraph 853 before you. The fact that he was a leader aggravates the offences. Again, the very factor the Prosecution says the Trial Chamber erred in failing to assess properly was the very factor that the Trial Chamber assessed. The law of aggravating factors is perfectly clear in this Tribunal. The obligation is upon the Prosecution to prove a aggravating factor beyond a reasonable doubt when it relies upon aggravation to enhance sentence. So in trying to prove military powers and political powers, it's the obligation of the Prosecution to prove those powers to the extent that it argues that they they're aggravating factors beyond a reasonable doubt. Again a very uncomfortable position for the Prosecution to assert given the acquittal by the Trial Chamber of Mr. Kordic under Article 7(3), an acquittal which we in our respectful submission was absolutely inevitable given the evidence which I'll go over in just a minute. Kordic's position as the vice-president of the Presidency of the HZ HB. What military powers did this position have? None. None whatsoever. What powers did it have? Well, the powers of a vice-president of the Presidency were purely parliamentary and how do we know that? Two things. First, the Prosecution's own constitutional law expert, Dr. Ciril Ribicic stated precisely that. Second, Dr. Ribicic explained that the Presidency of the HZ HB consisting not simply of the president, two vice-presidents, Bozo Rajic and Mr. Kordic, a secretary, Mr. Kostroman, and 31 heads of HVO civilian municipalities, that was the Presidency, that was the legislature of this nascent organisation. All of the constitutive documents, Your Honours, comprising the HZ HB, all the documents that explained how the institutions of the HZ HB worked were before the Trial Chamber, D181/1. Including the code of practice on the work on the Presidency which showed that the powers of the vice-president in the absence of the president of the Presidency being present were things like allocating the amount of time given to a person to speak. These were purely parliamentary powers. The vice-president of the Presidency had no military powers and Dr. Ribicic again conceded this. Mate Boban was the president of the HZ HB. He was the Supreme Commander of the HVO. And indeed none other than Perica Jukic who was the deputy Prime Minister of the HR HB confirmed the importance of distinguishing between those two offices. If I may request a brief private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. General Blaskic's second in command, Major General Filipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic have any military duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as command and control system are concerned, he was not involved at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, the commander of the military police. I know we've been over this but it bears going over one more time. Who appointed Colonel Palavra to his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was General Blaskic. Colonel Palavra testified that the military police were subordinate to the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in the normal vertical hierarchical fashion that one would expect in the chain of command. Colonel Palavra testified that he received his orders from his superior, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You received your orders strictly from the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. And the Appeals Chamber will remember this, this was a Court Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness summoned by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take any orders directions or instructions from Dario Kordic ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
