utterances.text: Your Honours, no, never. Said Colonel Palavra. No one has ever suggested that the Jokers were ever under the authority or command in any way of Mr. Kordic, he agreed. He also agreed that that also included his deputy Vladimir Santic, a person who never tried to contend to Colonel Palavra that Mr. Kordic was in any way involved with the military police. And then finally the proposition was put to Colonel Palavra by me that Mr. Kordic had no command authority whatsoever, any kind of superior subordinate relationship with the military police. I asked him to agree with it and he said: "I would agree with this." This or that is how it was. And as I said yesterday, that is indeed how it was. Colonel Vukovic, the predecessor to Pasko Ljubicic: "I never received orders from political figures at any time. I had my own chain of command." Cease-fire negotiations. If Mr. Kordic was such a significant figure, a integral figure involved in the chain of command who had to give the green light to military operations, the Appeals Chamber may well ask itself, why was this person not involved in any cease-fire negotiations. Consider this testimony, Your Honours. Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, with respect to the Novi Travnik fighting: "No one asked Kordic to attend or thought it would be important for him to attend the cease-fire negotiations?" "Correct. I wanted Blaskic there every time," insisted Colonel Stewart, the BritBat commander on the ground. We've explained and shown to the Appeals Chamber how the military chain of command worked in the expected routine hierarchical fashion that is normal in military organisations. D83/1, D84/1, and Exhibit Z715 show exactly how the chain of command worked, ironically in April of 1993, from the Supreme Commander who issues cease-fire orders as a result of a agreement with Mr. Izetbegovic, passed down to the Main Staff. The Main Staff receives those orders. Those orders are passed down to the Operative Zones and in the case of Exhibit Z615, the Operative Zone commander of that zone, General Blaskic, issued orders to all of the subordinate brigades under his command, including the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down. Would the counsel please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's very simple, and again we're informed of this by Lieutenant Colonel Stewart. We didn't need him, Kordic, to attend because we had the military commander's representative there. Did Mate Boban, the president of the HZ HB ever delegate any military authority to anybody? Again the evidence on that is uncontroverted. No. And it came from Srecko Vucina who was the head of the office of the president. I'd like to take a temporary detour to remind the Appeals Chamber, I'm sure it does not need to be reminded in detail, but to raise the issue that significant influence of a civilian is not in itself sufficient to result in the imposition of criminal liability without evidence that the civilian superior somehow had the ability to exercise control over military forces. This is recognised in the judgement, and indeed, paragraph 424 of the judgement is a accurate recitation of the law. In the case of civilian leaders, evidence of perceived authority may not be sufficient. It may be indicative of mere powers of influence in the absence of a subordinate structure. As the Naletelic Trial Chamber put the question poignantly, the question for a Trial Chamber and for this Appeals Chamber is the actual possession or non-possession of the power to control, yet here we have a finding from the Trial Chamber in paragraph 840 that there was no power on the part of Mr. Kordic to control HVO forces, and I might emphasise to the Appeals Chamber that this is a finding that has not been appealed by the Prosecution, and given the evidence we've just reviewed, it is Kordic's submission that that's for very good reason. Any appeal of that particular finding would be a dead duck from the -- from the starting post. Let's take a look at the HVO. What position did Mr. Kordic exercise in the HVO? Again, the evidence on that is uncontroverted. He had no position in the government of the HVO. The Prime Minister was Dr. Jadranko Prlic. There were three vice-presidents, Stipo Ivankovic, Kresimir Zubak, and Anto Valenta. So what position did Mr. Kordic occupy, if any, within the HVO? Again the evidence on that is clear. He was on the personnel committee of the HVO, a five-person committee headed up by the justice minister of the HZ HB, Zoran Buntic, and as you can see from the testimony on the screen, Mr. Buntic's testimony was that as far as he could recollect, that committee never met. May I have one more closed session for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Private?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Next position, president of the HDZ-BiH in Busovaca. True as far as it goes. He no longer occupied that position after April of 1992, and in Mr. Kordic's submission, the post that he occupied prior to April 1992 is of no material significance whatsoever to any of the findings made by the Trial Chamber or to any of the facts in this case. It was explained by Niko Grubesic that in fact after his resignation from that position he was replaced by Florijan Glavocevic for a brief time who was succeeded by Zoran Maric of the HDZ-BiH in Busovaca. Mr. Kordic attended meeting of the municipal government very seldom according to Niko Grubesic. President of the Travnik regional community. What was it? There was very little evidence presented by the Prosecution on what that was or what the powers of its president were. There was no proof at trial of what those powers were. It looks to have existed for just a few months and to have been a fairly informal organisation. Regional political leader in Central Bosnia. Well, this is sort of interesting. As the Appeals Chamber will recall, one of the proposals for peace in Central Bosnia was the Vance-Owen Plan which divided up central -- actually, all of Bosnia-Herzegovina into various cantons, and there was a structure proposed for a interim provincial government with a governor, a deputy governor, and then a governing council. In canton 10, the canton comprising Central Bosnia, there was a ten-person interim government structure proposed. If Mr. Kordic was the regional political leader in Central Bosnia, it might be expected that he would have been the proposed governor, but in fact he was not. The proposed governor was actually the mayor of Bugojno, Vladimir Soljic. Mr. Kordic was simply one of five Croat members of the proposed interim provisional government. There were four Muslim members of the proposed interim provisional government as I recall, and one Serb. Vice-president of the HR HB. This is perhaps the most baffling of the Trial Chamber's actual findings because it's not based on any legitimate evidence for the reasons I will go into right now. No such office existed and the Prosecution's constitutional law expert testified to that. Dr. Ribicic was asked to agree that there was no such office, such as there has been in the HZ HB, and he said: "That's right, yes." Again, it fell to Kordic to put all of the constitutive documents relating to the foundation and organisation of the HR HB before the Trial Chamber which he did. That's the exhibit D183/1 series. No office of vice-president provided for. Dr. Ribicic also acknowledged that Mr. Kordic was not a member of the HR HB government, nor was he a member of the presidential council. In fact, Perica Jukic who was a member of that council stated specifically that Mr. Kordic had no role in the government of the HR HB other than being one of the legislators. Yet the judgement finds Kordic to be a vice-president, paragraph 761. Why? It relied exclusively upon a ECMM document, Exhibit Z 1311 prepared by Colonel Stutt in the Travnik reporting centre. Colonel Blaskic had supposedly told Colonel Stutt that Kordic was a vice-president, but when asked at trial whether he was, Colonel Stutt said: "Well, that's difficult to answer." His information came from Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic admitted to Colonel Stutt that he -- that Blaskic was not a politician, he hadn't followed the political process closely and he was just a soldier. And there was other confirming evidence, D143/1 on that. And Colonel Stutt actually conceded, well, we didn't really know what Kordic was. Sometimes it's embarrassing to ask someone what he is. So what was the error regarding aggravation here? What was proved beyond reasonable doubt such as to amount to an aggravating factor? Nothing. And indeed the only aggravating factor was the aggravating factor found by the Trial Chamber that Mr. Kordic was a political leader and paragraph 853 makes it perfectly clear that the Trial Chamber took that into account. With respect to the increased -- the relatively longer sentence of General Blaskic, we have no particular submissions to make other than to remind the Appeals Chamber of what we've said about this in our brief, that the two cases are different. Colonel Blaskic was held liable under Article 7(3). The period under which he was held liable was longer. He was held liable for more offences such as the Stari Vitez truck bomb, the attack on Grbavica. He was found liable for all of the offences that took place in the Kiseljak area. He was indeed the military commander of the entire area, and we simply rely upon the long line of authority and I'm sure that the Appeals Chamber is well aware of it. It's most recently summarised in Krstic just a month ago, that it's inappropriate to set down a definitive list of sentencing guidelines for future reference given that the imposition of sentence is a discretionary function that differs from case to case. In conclusion, Your Honours, it's our respectful submission that there's no discernible error here. There's been no showing of an abuse of discretion. The very heavy sentence imposed upon Mr. Kordic, assuming that all of the facts as found, whatever they were, in the judgement and assuming that all of the offences upon which he was convicted are factually justified which in our respectful submission they most certainly were not, then there's simply no demonstrated discernible error and no demonstrated abuse of discretion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No questions. I thank you for the contribution. Let us have the final break in this case now and after the break we will have 30 minutes of reply by the Prosecution and as scheduled, both accused will have the opportunity, of course optional, if they so want, to address the Appeals Chamber. We reconvene a quarter past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And the floor is open immediately for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have only a few brief points that I wish to make in reply. Firstly, we are perfectly cognisant that we have a heavy burden. We understand completely the burden that we have on the standard of review for an appeal on sentence, and our arguments that the sentence imposed was manifestly inadequate was aimed at demonstrating that the Trial Chamber had made this discernible error in the exercise of its sentencing discretion by imposing this 25-year sentence, and the three bases were the gravity point, including his role, and of course, by failing to take into account his political leadership, together with the military authority that he so obviously wielded in the region. And not for one moment can our position be seen as inconsistent with our equal recognition of the principle that Trial Chambers exercise a considerable amount of discretion in determining an appropriate sentence or the recognition of the principle of individualisation of sentencing. Briefly on his arguments about gravity. Our main point, of course, is that despite the references, despite the reference in the judgement to the gravity of these crimes, and Kordic's criminal culpability, in our submission, the very sentence imposed shows that the Trial Chamber only played lip service to the gravity concept in sentencing him, and I rest completely on the submissions we made this morning in our appeal, as well as in our reply brief. Turning to the second basis, the positions and powers and his abuse of those positions and powers. Most of his arguments today were concentrated really on just an attempt to re-litigate the factual findings which were found by the Trial Chamber, and the point of our appeal that this is an aggravating factor, we based our sentence appeal on the factual findings as found by the Trial Chamber, both as to the contours of his political leadership and most importantly the parameters of his military authority or influence as found by the Trial Chamber. And I briefly referred this morning to the findings of the judgement. I'd also like to refer Your Honours to our lengthy description of these powers, positions, which we set out in our Prosecution Appeal Brief at pages 58 to 64, which set out the concrete and specific findings on his position, powers, and responsibilities and the role he was able to play as a result. And what Mr. Sayers did this afternoon was basically to refer to matters or to evidence which was considered by the Trial Chamber and rejected in reaching its actual factual findings. And especially when it came down to the question of his military authority. Again, I can't stress more highly our sentence appeal is based on the Trial Chamber's very own factual findings as to his role in military matters, and it isn't that we haven't failed to grapple with the difference between 7(1) and 7(3) responsibility, and nor is it an attempt by us to try and appeal his acquittal for 7(3) responsibility. When you come to consider the majority of his arguments this afternoon, we're not asking you to consider in aggravation of his criminal conduct any notion which is linked to his failure to prevent or punish crimes committed by soldiers under Blaskic's command. Our point is different. The principle underlying why a commander should, under 7(3), bear a higher sentence is equally apposite in a case like this when he holds a position of superior political authority and especially when he also exercised significant military authority and abused that position that those powers, by playing the role that he did in the planning and the ordering of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On this basis, Your Honours, you should find irrelevant all of his submissions this afternoon regarding the evidence that he drew your attention to, the witnesses he referred you today, Filipovic, Palavra, Vukovic, because their evidence went to the question of his military command in a sense of military duties, de jure sense. The Trial Chamber's findings as to his military authority, and we see the combination of this in paragraph 767, supported by paragraph 768, they're not the same as its findings on his military duties, which these witnesses attested to. And again, I refer you to all of the concluding factual findings the Trial Chamber made about his military authority. And they're all throughout the judgement. Regarding the political titles, the titles or functions he may have held, once again, we rely strictly on the Trial Chamber's findings on this point, and we point out that it's not a matter of blithe reference to some sort of -- it's not a reference just to the title itself, but it's to the function and the authority and the power which was expressed, which he was able to express in performance of those titles. And if the respondent now wishes to go back and re-litigate, ask the Appeals Chamber to re-look at all of that evidence, I'd simply point Your Honours, for a very full breakdown of his titles and the different functions he held throughout the time period, to annex 10 of the Prosecution closing brief, which presents a very detailed elaboration of this issue. How best can it be expressed? The line in paragraph 829: "He was the political leader of the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia." Turning briefly to the points he makes about disparity, or rather, that it's not relevant to look at Blaskic's sentence or to compare Kordic's sentence to Blaskic's. Of course, we see some distinctions between Kordic's and Blaskic's cases and their convictions. But several features of the case make it so clearly and directly relevant when you consider Kordic's case, not just the similarity of crime base, but also the fact that even though there's no conviction, Kordic bears no conviction under 7(3), his guilt under 7(1) is really as being the perpetrator behind the perpetrator, for having planned and ordered the crimes committed by the soldiers under Blaskic's command. And the final point: The Trial Chamber has made specific findings regarding the relationship between Kordic and Blaskic and concluded that it was either one of subordination or at least as co- or joint authorities. Our point is that there should not be any grave disparity between the final sentences imposed upon these two offenders, Kordic and Blaskic. And as a final point, the respondent has analysed the Tribunal jurisprudence to date as if it is uniformly or somehow against the utility of parity arguments on sentencing or when it comes to the Appeals Chamber's review of sentencing. Of course, we recognise that a sentencing range in this Tribunal is still in a nascent stage, but a range is beginning to emerge, but it's still at the more beginning stages, especially for certain types of crimes and offenders. One can't determine precisely with certainty for particular offences and offenders what a sentence exactly should be. And, true, the Appeals Chamber has rejected parity arguments in some cases, but it hasn't discounted the utility of comparing one sentence with another. And in fact, in some appeals cases, specifically Furundzija and Jelisic, the Appeals Chamber has specifically acknowledged the assistance which can be drawn from such a comparison in the very case like this, when the circumstances of the offences and the offender are substantially similar. And clearly, there's a value of having consistency in a sentencing for any criminal justice system and that would clearly include the justice system before this Tribunal. That completes my submissions, unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Brady. Mr. Farrell, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly respond to the -- or sorry, reply to the response by my learned colleagues, counsel for Mr. Cerkez. I don't think there's any misunderstanding by my friends, but it's a Prosecution appeal based on facts as found. My learned friends proceeded on the basis that there was no plan, that Mr. Cerkez wasn't involved, as if he wasn't even convicted for the any events in Donja Veceriska or Stari Vitez or Vitez. They proceeded to challenge the evidence that was before the Court and essentially argue in a sense that the Trial Chamber actually got it all wrong. That may be their position, but the issue on the Prosecution appeal is on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, did get it all wrong, for a different reason, the fact that they should have convicted him as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. There's a few points I wanted to make, procedural matters. There was essentially they reiterated their ground of appeal in relation to one of the documents, Z692.3. It doesn't actually answer the Prosecution appeal in the sense of indicating why, based on the findings of the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber was correct in concluding that he wasn't guilty for Ahmici. As my friend has indicated, there's lots of evidence that can be put before you or there is evidence that can be put before you to rebut his claims, but the bottom line is he's got to prove in his own appeal that the document shouldn't have been admitted. If he doesn't and we move to the Prosecution appeal on sentence then it's taken as a fact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that that document can be relied upon. He's indicated the relation to that document that there is other evidence, AT indicated that the direction of the attack of the Vitez Brigade was towards Sivrino Selo, the very next document referred to by the Trial Chamber, paragraph 689(D), talks about the artillery constantly attacking Sivrino Selo. I note that counsel for Mr. Cerkez has not challenged in terms of its authenticity this document. And the war diary indicates on April 18th at 12.02 that there was a request made of Mario, asking him to open fire on Sivrino Selo. And this provides support for Pasko, because they were outside Sivrino Selo. Counsel for Mr. Cerkez indicated that the Prosecution was changing its case. Gone from changing the case in the indictment in pre-trial brief to now changing the case on the appeal. And my learned friend referred to some passages from the opening in which he quoted, if I wrote it down correctly, that Cerkez was involved with his men in part of an overall plan but was not the particular brigade going in first thing that morning. That's exactly what the Trial Chamber found. He also says, and he quoted from submissions at trial, that Cerkez was part of the plan and played a role. Prosecution's closing brief. That is the Prosecution's position. It hasn't changed. Those are the findings of the Trial Chamber and that's the basis upon which he should have been found guilty. There was a comment by counsel for Mr. Cerkez that Mr. Cerkez had offered to cooperate with the Prosecution and testify in the Hadzihasanovic case. This matter, in my respectful submission, should have been brought as a 115 motion and the Prosecution would have been able to file evidence in response. But the Prosecution's submission is that to the extent that counsel for Mr. Cerkez did make such an offer, the assessment by the Office of the Prosecution was that it had very serious concerns about the truthfulness of whatever he would tell us, the scope he would agree to speak about, and that he was rejected outright as a potential witness. Therefore, we didn't even get to the point of determining whether or not he could provide any cooperation whatsoever, because the Prosecution declined that at the beginning. So the extent to which it's placed before you to show any type of cooperation under Rule 108, I would respectfully submit it doesn't even meet the requirements to be placed before you and certainly is not substantial cooperation under Rule 108.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause to give the interpreters a chance to catch up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There were a number of factual arguments that were raised, as I've indicated, arguments that there was no plan, that there was no knowledge on Mr. Cerkez's part, that there were no crimes, and that in fact the crime in Ahmici was described as a military operation which escalated to crimes during the fighting in the battles in the military operations that were occurring in Ahmici at the time. We respectfully request that you -- and considering the Prosecution's appeal, consider the findings and not the submissions of counsel. At the end of the day, the findings are irrefutable that there was a plan. It is inconceivable that an attack could take place of this magnitude, in this many villages, with the exact same pattern, over a hundred people killed, thousands of people detained, destruction extensively in relation to only one set of people, the Muslim people, Croat houses untouched. It's inconceivable that this could be somehow just a coincidence that it all happened at the same time by independent units, without any knowledge of the others, at 5.30 in the morning with the exact same illegal plan resulting in the exact same deaths, with no preparation and no ability to detain people once the attacks had happened because they hadn't planned it. With respect, it's quite clear even without Witness AT that there was a plan. It's quite clear that the findings of the Trial Chamber that there was a plan, that Mr. Cerkez had deliberately and intentionally acted pursuant to the plan, that he knew what his role was, he performed that function, and that he contributed significantly to the illegal campaign of persecution. In my respectful submission, there's only one conclusion that can be reached on the facts as found, if the law is applied correctly, and that is that this Appeals Chamber substitute a verdict of conviction on Mr. Cerkez for the counts as listed in the Prosecution's Appeal Brief for the crimes committed in Ahmici. That ends the Prosecution's appeal, Your Honours. Thank you for your patience. My apologies to the translators for the usual speed at which we speak. Subject to any questions, that would be the end of the appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no questions. In fact, the end of the appeal. We can note as the final points on the agenda and this is the invitation by the Appeals Chamber to both accused to address the Bench. However, before continuing, I want to emphasise that this final word should not be confused with Rule 84 bis. It's a possibility, an option, for an accused to address the Bench on whatever issue he so wants, and it's for the Bench to get a personal impression of the accused being not a mere object of criminal proceedings, but also a subject of these proceedings. Therefore, this right of having the final word will be granted, but, of course, only if the accused so wants. And the only thing what Rule 84 bis and the final word have in common is that an accused shall never be compelled to make such a final word and shall not be examined about the content of the statement. So may I ask first the Kordic Defence, in light of this: Did you discuss this with your client, and what is the position of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have. And Mr. Kordic's decision is that he does not wish to address the Bench. But one final matter is the neglected matter of the table that Mr. Smith referred to. As I understand it, the Prosecution has no objection to submitting this. So with the Court's permission, I'll give it to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so. So I understand, Mr. Kordic, that you waive your right to present a final word. THE APPELLANT KORDIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for showing such kindness to me. I do waive my right. I completely agree what my distinguished lawyers have put forward throughout this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I ask Defence of Mr. Cerkez, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I informed my client about the possibility, he was glad that he would finally have opportunity to say only briefly a couple of words about his attitude towards these proceedings, and he would be delighted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that we can really all together can follow your words, would you please stand up and proceed and stand in front of the witness stand. You are not acting as a witness. It's the final word of you in your capacity as an accused. Please. THE APPELLANT CERKEZ: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to thank you for giving me this opportunity to address you at the end of these long proceedings. The first thing I wish to say is that the only plan I had, Your Honours, on the 15th of April, 1993, was to marry my wife Slavica in church. My commander, Blaskic, was aware of this. This is the truth, Your Honours. I wish to tell you right away that I'm not trying to evade my part of the responsibility for everything that happened during the conflict between the Bosniak Muslims and the Croats in my native town of Vitez. In spite of the broad indictment with respect to time and area, all the bad things that happened, happened over a few days in April 1993, in only a few locations within the boundaries of Vitez municipality. Your Honours, I wish here to express in public my deep and sincere remorse and regret for every victim that resulted from the unfortunate conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats in the Lasva River Valley in 1993. I am aware that this will not assist the victims, but I do hope that their families and friends will accept my sincere expression of regret. I am aware that many people were killed, that many people were victims, to a greater or lesser extent, that many lost their homes, without any justifiable reason, and sometimes beyond the scope of military operations. For all this, I express my deep regret, and I believe that I have to bear a part of the responsibility for this, for the simple reason that I was a soldier on one of the sides in the conflict. This conflict was a necessary consequence of other events beyond my control and influence, and I'm sorry I took part in it. Your Honours, I feel responsible for everything that happened from the 16th of April, 1993, to the 21st of April, 1993, in the area of responsibility for which I was responsible. This was precisely stated in the order by the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Blaskic, who, on the 16th of April, 1993, at 1.30 in the morning, issued an order. This order, Your Honours, is one you have seen during these proceedings, D60/2. This order clearly set out my area of responsibility for which I'm responsible, as the commander of the Vitez Brigade during those few crucial days. Your Honours, you have seen that Blaskic, whose command was in Vitez, issued written orders on the 16th of April, 1993 to all existing units of the HVO in the area of Vitez, and that every order precisely established the area of responsibility for each unit. I did not issue these orders. Moreover, never, never did I issue an order to the Vitezovi or the 4th Battalion of the military police. I accept all responsibility for everything that happened in my area of responsibility. The Vitez Brigade, which was being established, which had existed for only 23 days, received an order that it was to prevent a possible attempt by the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the village of Kruscica and Vranjska, stage a breakthrough towards the town of Vitez. Your Honours, the village of Kruscica is my village, where my family lived, my parents, my wife, and my children. I carried out this order to the best of my ability in the given circumstances. Witness Anto Bertovic, and other witnesses, testified to this in detail. The soldiers under my command were deployed on several strategic positions between the village of Kruscica, Vranjska, and the town of Vitez. However, there was no attempt at a breakthrough by the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor did I order my soldiers to attack these forces in Kruscica and Vranjska. Your Honours, on the 21st of April, 1993, I received an order from Commander Blaskic that I was to set up sectors stretching along the edges of the municipality of Vitez, and this line of defence remained stable until the Washington Accords were signed in the spring of 1994. Throughout this time, the soldiers subordinate to me held this line of defence and repulsed many attacks by the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which undoubtedly had a plan to take the Lasva River Valley and especially the town of Vitez, because of the explosives factory that was located there. This was one of the largest factories of this type on the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There is no information showing that any crime was committed in this long period, from the 21st of April, 1993, to the end of September 1993, covered by the indictment. Your Honours, it is not my intention to mount a defence before Your Honours by stating this. My only wish in stating this was to show that, as a soldier and as the commander of the Vitez Brigade, I carried out the orders given to me in the locations specified in these orders. Your Honours, as a soldier, I consider that I can be responsible only for those areas on which soldiers under my command acted. In the indictment, there is no assertion that any crime happened in the areas and at the time while I was responsible there. Your Honours, when I learned of this indictment, after brief preparations for defence, I voluntarily appeared before this Tribunal. I knew what I was charged with. I knew I had not committed the crimes I was charged with, nor had soldiers subordinate to me committed them. I knew, therefore, that I would be able to defend myself. Your Honours, I wish to remind you that the HVO organised a civilian and a military component in about 40 municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Every municipality had a so-called "R" brigade. These were reserve units based on call-up of reservists. I was the commander of one such R brigade. Not a single commander of the municipal brigades of the HVO has been indicted before this Tribunal except for me. Unfortunately, in the municipality to which my brigade belonged, a crime occurred, the crime in Ahmici. This crime led to an investigation and an indictment and was the focal point of this trial. I was acquitted of this crime because the Trial Chamber established that my unit had not been at that location at that time. Let me repeat: I voluntarily appeared before the Tribunal, knowing I would not be convicted for that crime because I believed that the truth would become clear, and that's how it was. Your Honours, as a Croat from Bosnia and a member of the HVO, I am ashamed and hurt by the fact that in the area of the Lasva Valley, the HVO is responsible for several crimes. I'm referring primarily to the crime in Ahmici. Of course, I do not accept collective guilt as the basis for a criminal conviction, but I do accept moral responsibility for events which should not have happened. My only consolation is that I was neither able to prevent this as a soldier, nor as a human being. My consolation is also that such crimes were not committed by men under my command. Your Honours, I was born and brought up in a traditional environment, in which there was no ethnic or religious intolerance. Among my closest friends, there were Bosniak Muslims, Serbs, Roma, and others. I always evaluated people by their standpoints and their behaviour, not by their affiliation to a religion or an ethnic group. That is how I was brought up in my home, in school, in society, and that is what I always adhered to. In my previous life, nothing had prepared me for the wars that were waged in Bosnia from 1992 to 1994. When the war in Bosnia broke out in 1992, like many others belonging to my ethnic group, I was confused and frustrated, unable to understand the situation and the causes of the war. I personally support the fundamental idea which led to the establishment of this Honourable Tribunal. I support the efforts to bring to justice and convict individuals who committed crimes during the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that the stamp of collective guilt, the stigma of collective guilt, would not be borne by entire ethnic groups and nations. This is one of the reasons I surrendered voluntarily to this Tribunal. Your Honours, I wish to say that not a single witness before this Honourable Tribunal said anything against me as a person. On the contrary; many Bosniak Muslim witnesses, and others, said they did not think I was a person with ethnic prejudices. I was consoled by this, and this made it easier for me to bear these seven long years in prison. In my pre-war life, I was an average citizen. I completed vocational secondary school. I was employed first in municipal administration and then in the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory. I was never found guilty of a misdemeanour, let alone a crime. In Vitez, I got married. I have three daughters. My youngest, Marijana, is now in primary school. My two eldest daughters are at university. My eldest daughter Brankica is married and has a son and is now expecting a second child. In spite of this, she is a good student and she will soon get her degree, as will her husband. My middle daughter, Nikolina, is a student at the second year at the faculty of law in Split. After the war, I moved with my family to the beautiful town of Split in Croatia. My wife and I made this decision only due to a wish to ensure a better future for our daughters. In Bosnia, we no longer saw such a possibility. Your Honours, I'm sure you will understand that my time in detention has been very difficult, especially because of the suspense that detention entails. I have managed to transcend all this because of the good and healthy relations my family members have with each other and because of my faith that I will be acquitted of crimes for which I'm not responsible, and because of the art of painting that I have been engaged in in the last three years. What is most difficult is that I have not been able to spend the most beautiful years of my daughters' childhood with them. That is something that I have missed and that I will never be able to make up for. This is already a punishment, and this will remain even if this Honourable Tribunal should acquit me on every count. Finally, Your Honours, it is up to you to reach a just decision on my culpability and my sentence. I believe that you will weigh every piece of evidence with wisdom and care, both exculpatory and otherwise. I am sure that you will reach a just decision. Of course, I long for freedom and for a return to my beloved family. I can hardly wait for the day to be with my wife, my daughters, and grandchildren, to walk along the seafront in Split, in that beautiful town, by that beautiful sea, and to visit the rest of my family in the beautiful and mountainous country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, thank you for giving me this opportunity to express my thoughts in public, and I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cerkez. You may be seated again. This concludes now the appeal hearing in this case. It remains for me to thank everybody for the preparation of this case, in particular, all the parties, for their precise contributions, both in the pre-Appeal stage and during the hearing during the last three days. And also I have to thank all the staff members having prepared this hearing, and all the interpreters and the others behind the scene that made it possible to understand each other. I can't promise anything what about the time frame a judgement will be handed down. I think we are all aware of the complexity of the case, and I think it's in the interests of all parties that we try to be as precise as possible, and no doubt this will take some time. Once again, thank you, everybody, for this hearing. The hearing of this appeals stays adjourned until further notice.
